title: Art History in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe the big eras of art from cave paintings to today.
summary: The oldest known art is a hand stencil at least 67,800 years old, far older than writing. Art then moved through big eras, Stone Age to modern, each answering the last.

cards.headline: The oldest known artwork is a hand. It's at least 67,800 years old.
cards.body: Someone on Muna island, in Indonesia, pressed a hand to a cave wall and blew red ochre over it. Lift the hand away and its outline stays on the bare rock. It's still there. Art history starts with that hand, and this level runs from there to today.

cards.fact: If all of art history were one day, writing wouldn't show up until after 10 p.m.
cards.context: Squeeze the 67,800 years since that hand into 24 hours. Writing, invented about 5,200 years ago, appears just after 10 p.m.: for more than 22 hours, people made art but wrote nothing down. The Mona Lisa, begun about 1503, arrives about 11 minutes before midnight. Most of art's story happened before anyone could write about it.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: each era answers the one before.

cards.headline: Every era answers the one before
cards.body: Eras aren't just labels; they talk to each other. Renaissance is French for "rebirth": starting in 14th-century Italy, artists revived the ideas of ancient Greece and Rome. Centuries later, photography could record the world exactly, so painting no longer had to. Modern painters, starting in mid-1800s France, threw out the old rules. Each new era is partly a reply to the last one.

title: What Counts as Art?
objective: After this level you can explain why people have disagreed about what counts as art.
summary: In 1926 US customs taxed Brancusi's Bird in Space as metal because it didn't look like a bird. In 1928 a court ruled it art: art could express an idea, not just copy nature.

cards.headline: In 1926, US customs decided a famous sculpture wasn't art. Just metal.
cards.body: So they taxed it like any factory-made object. The fight that followed went all the way to court, where a judge had to settle a question people still argue about in galleries: what counts as art?

cards.headline: A bird with no wings
cards.body: The sculpture was Constantin Brancusi's Bird in Space. Picture a tall, slender strip of bronze, polished like a mirror. Brancusi left out the wings and feathers, stretched the body long and shrank the head and beak to a slanted oval. It doesn't show what one particular bird looks like. It's about the idea of flight.

mascot.line: Keep both tests handy. The question "what counts as art?" comes back later in this tree.

cards.headline: Two ideas of art collide
cards.body: Customs followed the old rule: a sculpture was carved or shaped in the likeness of natural models, like people and animals. No likeness, no sculpture. So they charged a 40% duty on it as a manufacture of metal. Brancusi's side said art could capture an idea instead. The critic Frank Crowninshield testified that it suggested flight, grace and speed, just as a bird does.
cards.callout: Old test: does it look like something? New test: does it express something?

cards.fact: In 1928, a court ruled that Bird in Space was art.
cards.context: The court noted a new school of art whose artists tried to portray abstract ideas rather than imitate natural objects, and said it had to be recognized. The ruling even admitted it might be hard to associate the thing with a bird. It was still pleasing to look at, and a work of art. The idea of art had moved, and the law moved with it.

title: The Artist's Toolkit
objective: After this level you can name the basic elements of art: line, shape, color, texture and space.
summary: Every artwork is built from the elements of art: line, shape, color, texture and space (many lists add form). Even empty space has a shape.

cards.headline: Every picture ever made uses the same few building blocks.
cards.body: A cave wall, a comic, the icon on your phone: artists build them all from what they call the elements of art. Learn five of them and you can take any picture apart.

cards.headline: Line and shape
cards.body: Start with line: a mark longer than it is wide. It can be straight or curved, thick or thin. Close a line into a loop and you have a shape. Shapes are flat and come in two families: geometric, like squares and circles, or organic, the free-form shapes you find in nature. A smiley face is one circle, two dots and a curve. Line and shape, doing all the work.

cards.headline: Color and texture
cards.body: Color is light reflected off things (Level 4 is all about it). Texture is how a surface feels, or looks like it would feel. It can be real, like thick paint you could touch, or only implied. A drawing of a porcupine can look prickly, but run your finger over it and the paper is smooth. The prickles are an illusion.

cards.fact: Empty space has a shape too.
cards.context: Space is the area around and between things. The empty part is called negative space, and it has a shape of its own: think of the hole in the letter O. Space also means the feeling of depth, when a flat picture seems to open up like a window. That's the five: line, shape, color, texture and space. Many lists add form, meaning 3D shapes like balls and boxes.

title: How Color Works
objective: After this level you can explain primary and complementary colors and how artists use them.
summary: Newton bent the spectrum into a color wheel. Red, yellow and blue are the painter's primaries; complements sit opposite, look more intense side by side, and mix to brown.

cards.headline: In 1824, the royal tapestry works in Paris had a problem: weak colors.
cards.body: The new head of dyeing at the Gobelins, a chemist named Michel-Eugène Chevreul, went looking for bad dye. He found something much stranger. To see what, you need a color wheel.

cards.headline: Newton bends the rainbow
cards.body: In his book Opticks, in 1704, Isaac Newton took the colors of the spectrum and bent them into a circle: an early color wheel. Painters use the idea to this day. Three colors sit at the heart of a painter's wheel: red, yellow and blue, the primaries. Every other color is a mix of them. Mix two primaries and you get a secondary: orange, green or violet.

cards.headline: Opposites on the wheel
cards.body: Colors directly across the wheel from each other are complementary: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Each pair shares no primary. Red is a primary, and green is blue plus yellow, so between them they use all three. Mix complements in paint and they cancel each other out into brown.
cards.callout: Red ↔ green · Blue ↔ orange · Yellow ↔ violet

mascot.line: Hold on to this one. Level 56's Impressionists and Level 63's Seurat both build on it.

cards.fact: A color changes depending on its neighbors.
cards.context: That was the Gobelins mystery. The dye was fine; the colors woven next to each other were changing how each one looked. Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839. Put complements side by side and each makes the other look more intense. His ideas went on to influence painters, including the Impressionists.

title: The First Artists
objective: After this level you can describe the oldest known cave art and how it was made.
summary: The oldest finds go from lines (a 73,000-year-old ochre crosshatch at Blombos Cave) to hands (stencils blown in ochre) to scenes (a picture story at least 51,200 years old in Sulawesi).

cards.headline: The oldest known drawing looks like a hashtag.
cards.body: It's a crosshatch of red lines on a small flake of stone from South Africa, about 73,000 years old. The earliest finds tell a story in three steps: first lines, then hands, then whole scenes.

cards.headline: Step 1: lines
cards.body: The flake comes from Blombos Cave. Someone drew on it with a pointed crayon of red ochre, an earth pigment that gets its color from iron oxide. It's at least 30,000 years older than any other known drawing. Is it art? Researchers still disagree. The lines might mean something, or they might just be left over from sharpening the crayon.

cards.headline: Step 2: hands
cards.body: Remember Level 1's hand, at least 67,800 years old? To make a stencil, you press your hand to the rock and blow pigment over it, sometimes through a pipe. Lift your hand and its outline stays. On Muna island, someone later went back and narrowed the fingers, turning a human hand into something closer to a claw.

mascot.line: You don't need the exact ages. Remember the order: lines, then hands, then a scene.

cards.fact: The oldest known picture story is at least 51,200 years old.
cards.context: On a cave wall at Leang Karampuang, also in Sulawesi, three human-like figures interact with a wild pig. It's not one animal on its own: it's a scene, the earliest known narrative art. Its age comes from thin mineral crusts that formed on top of the paint, dated by the uranium in them.

title: Lascaux and Chauvet
objective: After this level you can describe the animal paintings in the caves of Lascaux and Chauvet.
summary: Lascaux (about 17,000 years old) has huge black aurochs and closed in 1963 after visitors harmed it. Chauvet (about 35,500 years old) is full of lions, rhinos and mammoths.

cards.headline: In 1994, cave explorers in France felt a faint draft from a pile of stones.
cards.body: Behind it was a cave sealed by rockfalls for at least 21,000 years. On its walls: cave lions, woolly rhinos and mammoths. But first, meet an older discovery: Lascaux.

cards.headline: Lascaux: the Hall of the Bulls
cards.body: Four teenagers found Lascaux in 1940. Radiocarbon dating of its charcoal says about 17,000 years old. In its most famous room, four huge black bulls (aurochs) sweep across the rock, some about 5 meters long. Their bodies are drawn from the side, but their horns twist toward you, so you see both at once. The painters built scaffolding to reach the ceiling.

cards.fact: Lascaux lasted about 17,000 years in the dark, then about 15 years of tourists.
cards.context: It opened to visitors in 1948, up to 100,000 a year. Their traffic and the artificial lights faded the colors and brought algae, bacteria and crystals. In 1963 it closed. Since 1983, visitors have toured a replica nearby instead.

cards.headline: Chauvet: twice as old
cards.body: Radiocarbon dates put most of Chauvet's art at about 35,500 years old, roughly twice Lascaux's age. Its artists chose dangerous animals: among over 400 animals of 14 species are cave lions, woolly rhinos, mammoths and bears. They scraped walls clean, strengthened outlines and smudged charcoal to shade. In the End Chamber, a pride of lions hunts bison.

title: The First Sculptures
objective: After this level you can describe early carved figures and what they may have meant.
summary: The Lion-Man, carved in mammoth ivory about 40,000 years ago, mixes lion and human. Small figures of women, like Hohle Fels and Willendorf, have unknown meanings.

cards.headline: About 40,000 years ago, someone carved a creature nobody had ever seen.
cards.body: It stands upright like a person, but it has the head of a cave lion, and it's carved from a mammoth's tusk. Meet the Lion-Man.

cards.headline: The Lion-Man
cards.body: He was found in Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in Germany and stands 31 cm tall, about the length of a school ruler. That makes him the largest known sculpture of Ice Age art. When a modern experimenter carved a copy with Ice Age-style stone tools, it took hundreds of hours. That's a lot of time to spend on something you can't eat, wear or hunt with.

cards.headline: Small women, carved to hold
cards.body: The Venus of Hohle Fels, from another German cave, is mammoth ivory, 6 cm tall and 35,000 to 40,000 years old. Instead of a head, she has a small pierced loop, so she may have been worn as a pendant. The Venus of Willendorf, found in Austria, is about 30,000 years old: 11.1 cm of limestone, tinted with red ochre. She has no face at all, only a pattern like a braid or a cap.

cards.fact: "Venus" isn't their name, and nobody knows what they meant.
cards.context: Modern scholars borrowed the name from the Roman goddess of love, a goddess from many thousands of years later. Ideas about Willendorf include a fertility figure, a good-luck charm and a mother goddess. And a 2022 study added a travel story: her stone likely came from near Lake Garda in northern Italy, across the Alps.

title: Stonehenge and Great Stones
objective: After this level you can explain what monuments like Stonehenge show about early societies.
summary: Stonehenge took hundreds of workers, stones from Wales and feasts drawing people from across Britain. Göbekli Tepe, about 11,500 years old, was built by hunter-gatherers.

cards.headline: Stonehenge's builders joined giant stones the way a carpenter joins wood.
cards.body: Picture a ring of huge upright stones on a grassy plain, with stone beams laid across their tops. The beams are slotted on with joints you'd normally find in furniture. Monuments like this tell you who built them: how many people, how organized, and what mattered to them.

cards.headline: Built by hundreds, over centuries
cards.body: Stonehenge began as a circular ditch and bank about 3000 BC; the stones went up about 2500 BC. The giant sarsens, about 25 tons each on average, came from about 25 km away. The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, more than 200 km away. Moving, shaping and raising them took hundreds of people. That's not a weekend project. That's a society working together.

cards.fact: Some pigs at Stonehenge-era feasts came from as far as north-east Scotland.
cards.context: At Durrington Walls, near Stonehenge, archaeologists have found over 38,000 animal bones. Pig teeth show animals raised in west Wales, northern England and north-east Scotland, then slaughtered at midwinter. Stonehenge itself is lined up with the Sun: at midsummer the sun rises beside the Heel Stone, and at midwinter it set through the tallest arch. People came from far away, at special times of year.

cards.headline: Göbekli Tepe: older than farming
cards.body: In southeastern Turkey, hunter-gatherers began Göbekli Tepe about 11,500 years ago, more than twice Stonehenge's age and before farming. Its T-shaped limestone pillars reach over 5 meters and weigh up to 50 tons. Some are carved with foxes, scorpions and lions. Others have arms and hands carved down their sides, meeting in front over a belt: giant stone people. Building together may have led people to settle, not the other way round.

title: Why Early People Made Art
objective: After this level you can compare the main ideas about why early humans made art.
summary: Why early people made art is debated. Main ideas: an urge to record the world, hunting magic (with a reindeer problem), a spirit world, and keeping records.

cards.headline: Nobody left a note explaining the cave paintings.
cards.body: So researchers work from clues, and they disagree. The purpose of this art is still debated. Here are the main ideas. Hold them as ideas, not answers.

cards.headline: Idea: because people need to
cards.body: One view skips usefulness altogether: humans have a basic need to record and recreate the world around them. On this view the first artists drew for the same deep reason you doodle in a meeting. The catch is that it's hard to test.

cards.headline: Idea: hunting magic
cards.body: Maybe painting an animal was a kind of spell, to make a hunt succeed or herds multiply. It has a big problem at Lascaux. The bones left behind show the painters mostly ate reindeer, yet reindeer are almost absent from the walls. If you're casting a spell for dinner, you'd paint dinner.

cards.headline: Idea: a spirit world
cards.body: Most experts think cave art was symbolic or religious, sometimes both. One version: shamans entered trances to contact spirits, and the art shows that other world. Mixed creatures fit this idea, like Level 7's Lion-Man, or the Muna hand narrowed into a claw, which researchers think may reflect links between people and animals, or spiritual beliefs.

cards.fact: Some marks may be records, not pictures.
cards.context: Researchers suggest the patterns on an engraved ochre plaque from Blombos Cave may be a way of counting or storing information. Others wonder whether animals painted in their seasonal coats worked as an early calendar. The ideas don't have to compete: one cave could be a gallery, a temple and a notebook.

title: Checkpoint: The First Artists
objective: After this level you can describe the earliest known art and the main ideas about why it was made.
summary: Radiocarbon dates charcoal back to about 50,000 years; uranium-series dates crusts over mineral paint, giving a minimum age. That's why records say 'at least'.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: how do you date a painting nobody signed?
cards.body: Every date in this chapter came from a lab, not a label. Here's the whole chapter in order, then how those numbers were found, and why so many of them start with "at least".

events.label: An ochre crosshatch at Blombos Cave
A hand stencil on Muna island

cards.fact: Charcoal is a clock.
cards.context: Radiocarbon dating measures carbon-14 in things that were once alive, like the burnt wood in charcoal, and works back to about 50,000 years. Many of Chauvet's black lines are charcoal, so labs can date the drawings themselves: most are about 35,500 years old. At Lascaux, charcoal from the cave gives about 17,000.

mascot.line: Read "at least" as a floor, not a guess. The paint is older than the crust on top of it.

cards.headline: Why "at least"?
cards.body: Red ochre is iron oxide, a mineral, and many paintings have no organic material to date. So researchers date something else: thin mineral crusts that grew over the paint, using uranium, as at Leang Karampuang. The crust formed after the painting, so the paint must be older. That's a minimum age. The real one could be older, which is why records keep getting broken.

title: Mesopotamia
objective: After this level you can describe Mesopotamian art, from stepped temples to carved seals.
summary: Mesopotamian cities raised stepped mud-brick ziggurats, like Ur's for the moon god Nanna, and carved tiny stone cylinder seals that printed pictures on clay.

cards.headline: The first cities built their temples out of mud.
cards.body: Mesopotamia is Greek for "between rivers": the land of the Tigris and Euphrates, where the world's earliest civilization grew up. Its builders worked in brick, and its artists often worked in something humbler still: clay. This level runs from a temple tower down to a picture about the size of your thumb.

cards.headline: A staircase for a god
cards.body: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower. Picture a stack of ever-smaller brick platforms, like a giant wedding cake. The core was mud brick, wrapped in a tougher skin of baked brick. The best known, at Ur, went up about 2100 BCE under King Ur-Nammu for the moon god Nanna. Three staircases led up, and on the flat top sat a temple. The tower's whole job was to lift that temple up.

cards.fact: A cylinder seal prints a whole picture strip in one roll.
cards.context: Carve a design into a small stone cylinder, often no bigger than 5 cm tall, about the size of your thumb. Roll it across wet clay and the carving comes out raised, as one continuous band, the way a patterned paint roller works. Scholars count these tiny carvings among Mesopotamia's finest art.

cards.headline: A signature you could roll
cards.body: Seals weren't just decoration. Rolled onto clay, a seal marked what you owned or made a document legally binding: rolled on a tablet, it showed you had authorized the text, like a signature. Remember Level 1's writing, about 5,200 years ago? It was Sumerian cuneiform, wedge-shaped marks pressed into soft clay with a stylus. In Mesopotamia, words and pictures shared the same wet clay.

title: The Rules of Egyptian Art
objective: After this level you can explain the rules that kept Egyptian art so consistent for 3,000 years.
summary: Egyptian artists drew each body part from its most complete angle, used a shared 18-unit grid, and made important people bigger. The style held for about 3,000 years.

cards.headline: Egyptian art kept one look for about 3,000 years.
cards.body: It did change, slowly, but it held its character so well that you can spot Egyptian art from across a museum. The secret is rules. Learn three and you can read almost any Egyptian painting.

cards.headline: Rule 1: every body part at its best angle
cards.body: Stand like a figure in an Egyptian painting and you'd need a very flexible neck. The head is in profile, but the eye looks straight at you. The shoulders face front, while the legs walk sideways. This wasn't clumsiness: artists combined viewpoints to show each part of the body in its most complete form. Level 6's aurochs did something similar, with bodies from the side and horns turned toward you.

mascot.line: You don't need the number 18. Remember why the grid mattered: the same proportions every time.

cards.fact: A standing figure measured 18 squares from the soles of the feet to the hairline.
cards.context: Artists laid a grid on the wall first, so a body came out with the same proportions whatever its size. Why stop at the hairline? Crowns and headdresses varied, so the top of the head didn't count. Every workshop sharing one grid is part of why the style stayed so steady.

cards.headline: Rule 3: bigger means more important
cards.body: In a tomb painting, the king or the tomb owner towers over everyone. His family is smaller, his servants smaller still. It isn't distance; it's rank. Remember Level 1: Egyptian art served the king and the gods, and size told you at a glance exactly who mattered.

title: Art for the Afterlife
objective: After this level you can explain why Egyptians filled their tombs with art.
summary: Egyptians believed the ka, a life force, needed food forever, and that images could magically provide it. So tombs held painted food, models like Meketre's and shabti workers.

cards.headline: In 1920, archaeologists opened a room nobody had entered in almost 4,000 years.
cards.body: It was in the tomb of Meketre, an Egyptian official. Robbers had stripped the tomb long ago, but they missed one small hidden chamber. Inside, packed tight, stood 24 painted wooden models. Why would anyone bury a miniature world?

cards.headline: Food for the ka
cards.body: Egyptians believed each person had a ka, a life force that still needed food and drink after death. Real offerings run out. Pictures don't. So tombs were filled with scenes and models of food and food-making, which could feed the ka forever without ever being used up. A painted loaf is the one snack that never goes stale.

cards.headline: Meketre's model estate
cards.body: Meketre's models show boats, people carrying offerings, and workshops where craftsmen work and cooks make bread and beer. They look like toys. They weren't. Egyptians believed images could magically give the dead safe passage to the afterlife and food once there. Every tiny baker had a job: keep Meketre fed.

cards.fact: Some tomb figures were buried to do your chores.
cards.context: Shabtis were small figures of substitute workers, placed in tombs so they could do the dead person's labor in the afterlife. That fits the Egyptian dream: not a distant paradise, but daily life on Earth carried on, without the pain. Tomb art showed people as they wished to stay forever, which is why the tomb itself was called the ka house.

title: Greek Vases
objective: After this level you can explain black-figure and red-figure vase painting.
summary: Black-figure (Corinth, about 700 BCE) painted black figures and scratched in details. Red-figure (Athens, about 530 BCE) flipped it and painted details with a brush.

cards.headline: A Greek jar from about 540 BCE reads like a comic strip.
cards.body: The Greek heroes Achilles and Ajax sit facing each other, playing a dice game. Words run from their mouths: Achilles calls "four", Ajax calls "three". The painter, Exekias, signed it as both potter and painter. His figures are black on orange-red clay, and that color scheme is the key to this level.

cards.headline: Black-figure: paint the shape, scratch the detail
cards.body: Black-figure began in Corinth about 700 BCE, and Athens took it up by the end of the 7th century BCE. The painter filled in each figure in glossy black on the bare clay, then scratched fine details through the black with a sharp point. Think of scratch art, on a vase. Exekias's dice game is black-figure.

cards.fact: The black on a Greek vase isn't paint. It's clay.
cards.context: Painters used slip, a fine liquid clay. The color change happened in the kiln, in a three-stage firing that switched between letting air in and shutting it out. The slip came out glossy black, and the bare clay returned to orange-red. The painter had to picture the finished colors before the fire made them.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Black-figure: black figures, scratched detail. Red-figure: red figures, brushed detail.

cards.headline: Red-figure: the big flip
cards.body: In Athens, about 530 BCE, painters reversed the whole system. Now the background was painted black, and the figures were left in bare red clay. Details went on with a brush instead of being scratched. That small switch mattered: a brush curves and flows, so painters had more freedom to show bodies, movement and facial expressions. Red-figure went on to dominate.

title: Greek Sculpture
objective: After this level you can explain how Greek sculptors moved from stiff figures to lifelike bodies.
summary: Archaic kouroi stood stiff and frontal, in a pose reflecting Egypt. Just after 480 BCE the Kritios Boy shifted his weight onto one leg: contrapposto. Polyclitus then wrote the rules.

cards.headline: For generations, Greek statues stood at attention. Then one relaxed.
cards.body: Try it: stand with your weight on one leg, like you're waiting for a bus. Your hips tilt, your shoulders tilt the other way, and you look alive. Greek sculptors had to discover that.

cards.headline: Archaic: the kouros
cards.body: From about 615–590 BCE, Greek sculptors carved kouroi: stone statues of standing young men, some used as grave markers. Picture one facing straight ahead, left foot slightly forward, arms close to his sides, fists clenched. If he reminds you of Egypt, that's no accident: the kouros reflects Egyptian traditions, especially their body proportions. Remember Level 12's grid?

mascot.line: If you keep one word from this level, make it contrapposto: weight on one leg.

cards.headline: The Kritios Boy shifts his weight
cards.body: Just after 480 BCE, a marble youth from the Athenian Acropolis did something new. He rests his weight on his left leg, while his right leg relaxes, bent at the knee. That's contrapposto: one leg takes the load, so the hips, shoulders and head tilt. Weight on both legs looks like a statue. Weight on one looks like a person.

cards.fact: The Spear Bearer was a rulebook you could walk around.
cards.context: About 450–440 BCE, the sculptor Polyclitus made the Doryphoros, or Spear Bearer, to illustrate his book, the Canon, on the ideal proportions of the human body. His relaxed contrapposto helped free Greek sculpture from rigid, face-front poses. The stiff kouros had become a body at ease, measured to an ideal.

summary: Greek columns come in three orders: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian. The Parthenon, built from 447 BCE for Athena, is the peak of Doric, full of subtle curves still debated.

cards.headline: The Parthenon looks perfectly straight. It isn't.
cards.body: Its base bulges upward in the middle and its columns swell slightly. People have argued about why since Roman times. First, though, learn to read a Greek column from the top.

cards.headline: The Parthenon
cards.body: Built of white marble from 447 BCE and finished by 438 BCE, the Parthenon honored the goddess Athena. Its architects, Ictinus and Callicrates, worked under the sculptor Phidias, and they made it the high point of the simplest order, Doric. Simple, here, doesn't mean plain: almost nothing about this building is as straight as it looks.

cards.fact: The Parthenon's base rises about 5 cm in the middle.
cards.context: Its columns bulge slightly (entasis), and its corner columns are thicker. The classic explanation comes from the Roman architect Vitruvius: the curves correct optical illusions, so the temple looks straight. In 2026, the mathematician Alain Goriely argued there's no evidence the curves produce those illusions at all. The curves are measured fact; the reason is still an argument.

title: Roman Art
objective: After this level you can explain what Roman art borrowed from Greece and what it added.
summary: Rome copied Greek statues and borrowed the Greek orders, then added its own: warts-and-all portraits from around 100 BCE and the Pantheon's huge concrete dome.

cards.headline: We know Level 15's Spear Bearer only because Romans copied it.
cards.body: None of Polyclitus's original statues survive. The Doryphoros is known only through Roman copies. In the late Republic, admiring earlier Greek art became the fashion in Rome. So what did Rome add of its own?

cards.headline: What Rome borrowed
cards.body: Rome also borrowed Greece's architecture. The Romans adopted the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders you met in Level 16 and adapted them for their own buildings. So far, a very good student. But Rome also pushed in directions of its own.

cards.headline: Warts and all
cards.body: Level 15's Greeks measured out an ideal body. Roman portrait sculptors, flowering around 100 BCE, recorded every line, crease, wrinkle and even blemish. The style is called verism. It wasn't a lack of tact: especially for men, the wrinkles of age signaled dignity and authority, the face of experience. Imagine a politician's poster that proudly adds ten years.

cards.fact: The Pantheon's dome is about 43 m across, and it's concrete with no steel inside.
cards.context: The emperor Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon between 118 and 128 CE. Its unreinforced concrete dome was unmatched in scale until modern times. The only light comes through an opening about 8 m wide at the top, the oculus, The columns came from Greece. The dome was pure Rome.

title: Mosaics
objective: After this level you can explain how mosaics are made and where they flourished.
summary: Mosaics are pictures of small closely set tesserae. Greeks invented cut tesserae; Romans laid mosaic floors across the empire, like Pompeii's Alexander Mosaic.

cards.headline: A Pompeii doorway still says "Beware of the dog".
cards.body: At the entrance of the House of the Tragic Poet, a black dog on a chain is set into the floor in tiny pieces of stone, above the words CAVE CANEM. Vesuvius buried Pompeii in 79 CE, and the warning survived. It's a mosaic: a picture you could walk on.

cards.headline: Pictures made of dice
cards.body: A mosaic is built from tesserae: small, closely set pieces of stone, glass, tile or shell. The name is Latin for "cubes" or "dice". The Greeks refined floor pictures made of pebbles, then invented cut tesserae, shaped to fit tightly together. Tighter pieces meant denser, more detailed pictures, the way more pixels make a sharper photo.

cards.headline: The Alexander Mosaic
cards.body: In the House of the Faun, another Pompeii house, lay a floor about 5.8 m wide, made around 100 BCE from more than a million tesserae. It shows Alexander the Great fighting the Persian king Darius III at the Battle of Issus. Scholars believe it's a Roman copy of a lost Greek painting. If so, a great Greek painting survives only as a Roman floor.

cards.headline: Floors of an empire
cards.body: Roman mosaics spread throughout the empire as floor decoration. The same art covered a guard-dog warning at a front door and a great battle in the House of the Faun. Across the empire, Romans walked on pictures.

title: Early Art of China and India
objective: After this level you can describe the Terracotta Army and early Buddhist sculpture.
summary: About 8,000 clay soldiers, each with its own face, guard China's first emperor. In India, early art showed the Buddha only as symbols, until about the 1st century CE.

cards.headline: In 1974, farmers digging a well in China found an army.
cards.body: Underground stood about 8,000 life-size soldiers made of clay, buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 BCE. Meanwhile in India, sculptors faced the opposite puzzle: how do you show someone without showing him?

cards.headline: An army of individuals
cards.body: The soldiers weren't made in one piece. Each was assembled from separately fired sections, then given its own detailed face. Picture thousands of clay men, each with a face of his own. Their weapons, cast from an unusual metal alloy, are still shiny and sharp today. Their job: guard the emperor's tomb.

cards.headline: The Buddha as an empty seat
cards.body: At Sanchi, in India, stone gateways added to the Great Stupa in the 1st century BCE are crowded with carved stories of the Buddha's life. But look for the Buddha himself and you find only signs: a wheel, an empty throne, a pair of footprints. The story is all there; the star never appears. It's like a film where the hero is always just off screen.

cards.headline: Then the Buddha got a face
cards.body: Around the 1st century CE, sculptors in two places, Gandhara and Mathura, each began showing the Buddha in human form. Gandhara, in today's northwestern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan, made a version you might recognize: a youthful, Apollo-like face and robes like those on Roman imperial statues. Greek and Roman ideas had traveled a very long way.

cards.fact: Greek and Roman marble statues were once painted in bright colors.
cards.context: It's called polychromy, Greek for "many colors". Researchers find the faint traces with infrared and ultraviolet light. Weathering, cleaning, air and sunlight erased most of it, and what was left is the white stone we now call classical.

cards.headline: Color that vanishes in minutes

title: Byzantine Art
objective: After this level you can describe Byzantine icons and gold-backed mosaics.
summary: Byzantine artists set holy and imperial figures against gold glass, read as a spiritual realm. Icons, holy images on wooden panels, were banned from about 726 until 843.

cards.headline: In Ravenna, an emperor has stood in a sky of solid gold since 547.
cards.body: The emperor is Justinian, in a mosaic in the church of San Vitale, Italy. His empress, Theodora, faces him across the apse. There is no landscape and no room behind them, only gold. Byzantine artists weren't showing you where these people stood. They were showing you something else.

cards.headline: Gold made of glass
cards.body: Picture Justinian in a purple robe, with a halo round his head. He holds a golden paten, a dish for the church's bread. Across the apse, Theodora holds a chalice for the wine. And the gold behind them? It's glass: small cubes with a thin sheet of gold leaf sealed under clear glass. A whole wall of them glitters.

mascot.line: The key idea: the gold isn't a sky. It says this is no ordinary place.

cards.headline: Not a place on any map
cards.body: Why gold instead of sky? Art historians read it as a way of saying this is no ordinary place: the figures stand in a spiritual, otherworldly realm. That's also why they look flat and still, with stylized bodies. The goal was never to copy the world exactly. It was to show what believers held to be more real than the world.
cards.callout: Flat and gold on purpose: the setting is heaven, not a room.

cards.fact: The oldest known icon of Christ was painted in hot wax, in the 6th century.
cards.context: An icon is an image of a holy figure, usually painted on a wooden panel. This one, at Saint Catherine's Monastery in Sinai, was painted in encaustic, colored wax worked hot. Christ raises one hand in blessing and holds a jeweled Gospel book in the other.

cards.headline: The century of smashed images
cards.body: Believers said they didn't worship wood and paint: honor shown to an icon passed to the holy person it showed. Not everyone agreed. From about 726, Byzantine emperors condemned icon veneration as idolatry, and countless images were destroyed. Icons were restored for good in 843, and the Orthodox Church still celebrates it. The Sinai Christ survived because its monastery lay outside imperial control.

title: Islamic Art and Pattern
objective: After this level you can explain why Islamic art so often uses geometry, pattern and calligraphy.
summary: Mosques leave out images of people: creating living forms was held to belong to God. Instead come calligraphy, esteemed because the Qur'an came in Arabic, and endless geometry.

cards.headline: Walk into a great mosque and look for a picture of a person. You won't find one.
cards.body: Instead, the walls are covered in writing, curling vines and stars that seem to go on forever. That isn't because Islamic art never shows people. It's a choice about what belongs in a place of prayer.

mascot.line: A common mix-up: Islamic art does show people. It's the mosques that leave them out.

cards.headline: Why the mosque has no faces
cards.body: The reason is a belief: creating living forms belongs to God alone. The Qur'an calls God musawwir, the "maker of forms", and sayings attributed to the Prophet Muhammad warn painters who try to "breathe life" into images. Outside religious spaces it's a different story: people and animals turn up often in palaces and illustrated books. Islamic art isn't picture-free. Its mosques are.

cards.headline: Writing as the highest art
cards.body: If a place of prayer won't show holy people, what does it show? The holy word. Muslims believe the Qur'an is God's revelation to the Prophet Muhammad, and it was revealed in Arabic. So calligraphy, beautiful writing, became the most highly regarded Islamic art. It runs across mosque walls, bowls, metalwork and textiles. Here, the words are the picture.

cards.fact: The most complex Islamic patterns need only a compass and a ruler.
cards.context: Start with a circle, divide it, join the points with straight lines, and a star appears. Repeat that one unit side by side and the pattern can keep going in every direction, with no natural edge. Many scholars read that endlessness as suggesting infinity, and for some, the unity of God. It's an interpretation, but you can see why it sticks.

title: The Alhambra and Great Mosques
objective: After this level you can describe the architecture of the Alhambra and the great mosques.
summary: Córdoba's Great Mosque (begun about 785) is a forest of reused Roman columns under two tiers of striped arches. Granada's Alhambra, "the red one", is the Nasrid palace of the Court of the Lions.

cards.headline: In Córdoba, a mosque turned into a forest.
cards.body: Step into the prayer hall of the Great Mosque of Córdoba, in Spain, and columns run away from you in every direction, topped with arches striped red and white like candy canes. Then there's Granada's Alhambra, a palace built on a hill. Two buildings, two very different jobs.

cards.headline: Arches on top of arches
cards.body: The mosque was begun about 785 under the ruler Abd al-Rahman I. Many of its columns were reused from ancient Roman buildings. On top of them sits a second tier of arches stacked above the lower horseshoe arches, which gave the prayer hall greater height. The stripes come from alternating red brick and white stone. Recycling, with style.

cards.headline: The red one
cards.body: The Alhambra takes its name from Arabic al-Hamra, "the red one", after the reddish color of its walls. Its famous palaces were built in the 14th century by the Nasrids, the last Muslim dynasty to rule in Spain. At the heart is the Court of the Lions, built for the sultan Muhammad V from 1362. Its fountain basin rests on 12 carved marble lions.

cards.fact: The Alhambra repeats one sentence over and over on its walls.
cards.context: It's the Nasrid motto: "There is no victor but God." It's carved into the plaster again and again, woven among geometric stars and vines. Look up in the halls around the Court of the Lions and you'll find muqarnas, ceilings of many small niche-like cells, often compared to honeycomb. They're some of the most elaborate in the Islamic world.

title: Illuminated Manuscripts
objective: After this level you can explain how medieval scribes made illuminated manuscripts.
summary: Monks wrote books by hand on calfskin vellum, then laid on gold leaf and polished it to shine: that is illumination. The Book of Kells, about 800, is the most famous.

cards.headline: Illuminated manuscripts really do light up.
cards.body: Tilt a page from a medieval Gospel book and bits of it flash like a mirror. That's real gold. Every one of these books was written and decorated by hand, one page at a time. So how do you make a book that glows?

cards.headline: Step 1: a page made of skin
cards.body: The finest medieval books weren't written on paper but on vellum, a parchment made from calfskin. Most were made in monasteries. The scribe ruled faint lines across the page to keep the writing straight, then wrote with a sharpened quill or a reed pen. No delete key, so concentrate.

cards.headline: Step 2: gold that shines
cards.body: Then came the gold. Thin sheets of gold or silver leaf were laid onto a sticky ground, then polished to a shine with a smooth stone, or even a dog's tooth. Strictly, only a book decorated with gold or silver counts as illuminated (from Latin illuminare). Today the word covers any decorated manuscript.
cards.callout: Illuminated, strictly: decorated with gold or silver that catches the light.

cards.fact: The Book of Kells was made about 800, by monks, entirely by hand.
cards.context: Columban monks wrote the four Gospels in Latin on 340 vellum leaves. Work probably began on the island of Iona, off Scotland; after a Viking raid in 806, the monks moved to Kells in Ireland. Its famous Chi-Rho page is almost all one word: the Greek letters that begin "Christ", swelling into spirals and knots. Look closely and you'll find cats and mice in the decoration.

title: Romanesque Churches
objective: After this level you can describe thick-walled Romanesque churches and their round arches.
summary: Romanesque ("Roman-like") churches used round arches and heavy stone vaults, so walls were thick and windows small. Conques carved the Last Judgment over its door.

cards.headline: Romanesque churches look like fortresses. Blame the ceiling.
cards.body: Thick walls, small windows, dim insides: these churches can feel like castles for prayer. The reason isn't fear of attack. It's the heavy stone roof over your head, and what it does to the walls.

cards.headline: Roman-ish
cards.body: Romanesque means "Roman-like". Scholars coined the name in the 19th century for European art and building of about 1000 to 1150, because it borrowed from ancient Rome, above all the round arch. Remember Level 1? In the Middle Ages, Western art was mostly art for the church. These churches are where much of it lived.

mascot.line: Hold on to why these walls are so thick. Level 26 is the answer to this problem.

cards.headline: Why the walls are so thick
cards.body: Romanesque builders roofed their churches with barrel vaults: stone ceilings shaped like half a tunnel. All that stone pushes outward as well as down, so the walls had to be massive to hold it in. Big windows would weaken them. The result: thick walls, few small windows and often a dark interior. A stone tunnel with a few peepholes.

cards.fact: Over the door at Conques, a devil tries to cheat at the Last Judgment.
cards.context: Sainte-Foy at Conques, in France, was a stop for pilgrims walking to Santiago de Compostela in Spain, drawn by the relics of Saint Foy. Its tympanum, the half-moon panel over the door, was carved in the early 1100s with at least 124 figures. Christ sits in judgment. Below him, the archangel Michael weighs souls, while a devil presses on the scale.

title: Gothic Cathedrals
objective: After this level you can explain pointed arches and flying buttresses and why Gothic churches soar.
summary: From Saint-Denis in 1144, Gothic builders used pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses to carry the roof's weight elsewhere, so walls could be thin, tall and full of glass.

cards.headline: Gothic cathedrals are stone skeletons wearing glass.
cards.body: Level 25's churches needed thick walls to hold their roofs up. In 1144, near Paris, builders showed a way to send that weight somewhere else. Once the walls stopped carrying the roof, they could rise higher and open into windows.

cards.headline: An abbot who wanted light
cards.body: The abbey church of Saint-Denis, near Paris, is traditionally called the first Gothic building. Its abbot, Suger, saw light as a reflection of the infinite light of God, and he wanted his new choir, dedicated in 1144, filled with it. His masons brought together tricks that had been used separately: the pointed arch, the ribbed vault and large windows.

cards.headline: Three tricks for going up
cards.body: A pointed arch sends more of its weight down and less outward than a round one, so it can climb higher. A ribbed vault is a ceiling of stone ribs filled with thin panels: lighter, and it lands its weight on a few points instead of whole walls. Flying buttresses, half arches outside the building, carry the remaining push across to outer piers. The walls are off duty. So they can be glass.
cards.callout: Pointed arch + ribbed vault + flying buttress = thin walls, huge windows.

cards.fact: The tallest Gothic vault, at Beauvais, is about 48 meters high.
cards.context: Beauvais Cathedral in France pushed the system to its limit. In 1284 part of its choir vault collapsed. The builders rebuilt it at the same height, with extra supports. Gothic could soar, but it had to be braced.

cards.headline: A name meant as an insult
cards.body: The builders never called it Gothic. Italian Renaissance writers such as Giorgio Vasari used the word as an insult, after the Goths, whom they saw as the barbarians who helped destroy Rome. The name stuck. The scorn didn't.

title: Stained Glass
objective: After this level you can explain how stained glass windows were made and what they taught.
summary: Glass was colored with metal oxides, cut, painted, fired and joined with lead. Pope Gregory the Great defended pictures as teaching those who cannot read.

cards.headline: At the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, the walls are made of Bible stories.
cards.body: This royal chapel, consecrated in 1248, has 1,113 stained-glass scenes, so many that the walls seem to be made of glass. Level 26's flying buttresses freed walls to become windows. So how do you build a window from colored light, and why fill it with stories?

cards.headline: Color cooked into the glass
cards.body: Medieval glassmakers colored glass while it was molten, by adding metal oxides: cobalt, for instance, gives a deep blue. The glazier cut the colored sheets into pieces, painted faces and folds of cloth with a dark paint made partly of ground glass, and fired them in a kiln so the paint fused on. Strips of lead called cames held the pieces together, like a jigsaw with the joins left showing.

cards.fact: One window at Chartres survived the fire of 1194.
cards.context: Fire destroyed most of Chartres Cathedral in 1194. The central panels of the Virgin and Child in the window called Notre-Dame de la Belle Verrière, made about 1180, survived and were set into the new building. For centuries, this image of Mary has been an object of special veneration.

mascot.line: Keep this argument in mind: pictures teach people who can't read. Level 78 makes it again.

cards.headline: Pictures for people who can't read
cards.body: Why fill windows with stories? In a letter of 600, Pope Gregory the Great defended religious pictures: what writing gives those who read, a picture gives to those who can't. His argument remained the standard defense of religious images in the Western church through the Middle Ages. A window was a page anyone could read, as long as the sun was out.

title: Giotto
objective: After this level you can explain how Giotto made painted figures look solid and human.
summary: About 1305 Giotto frescoed Padua's Arena Chapel with blue skies instead of gold and figures with weight and feeling, as in the Lamentation. Dante noted his fame.

cards.headline: Dante put a painter in the Divine Comedy.
cards.body: Cimabue thought he held the field in painting, Dante wrote, but now the cry is for Giotto. Dante's real point was that fame fades fast. Still, it shows how quickly Giotto's name spread. What were people looking at?

cards.headline: A chapel painted wet
cards.body: About 1305, Giotto covered the walls of the Arena Chapel in Padua, paid for by the Scrovegni family, with scenes from the lives of the Virgin Mary and Christ. He painted in fresco: pigment brushed onto wet plaster, so the color dries into the wall itself. And behind his scenes he painted blue skies, not the traditional gold.

cards.headline: People with weight
cards.body: Remember Level 21's Byzantine figures, flat and stylized on their gold? Giotto broke with that. His figures have rounded, sculptural bodies with a clear sense of weight. They stand on the ground; you feel you could walk around them. And they show real feeling, which is where the next card comes in.
cards.callout: Byzantine: flat saints on gold. Giotto: solid people under a blue sky.

cards.fact: In Giotto's Lamentation, two mourners sit with their backs to you.
cards.context: The scene, painted about 1305, shows Christ's followers gathered around his dead body. In front, two figures turn away from us, so we look past them like someone at the back of a crowd. A rocky ridge slopes down toward Christ's head, and in the blue sky above, angels twist in grief. You're not looking at a symbol of mourning. You're at the funeral.

title: Chinese Landscape Painting
objective: After this level you can explain how Chinese painters used ink to capture mountains and mist.
summary: Shan shui ("mountain-water") painting flowered in the Northern Song. Fan Kuan dwarfed his travelers under a huge mountain; Guo Xi combined three distances; mist is often bare silk.

cards.headline: The most famous landscape in China hid its painter's name for centuries.
cards.body: It's called Travelers among Mountains and Streams, and the painter is Fan Kuan. You'll need a moment to find the travelers. Finding his signature took scholars far longer.

cards.headline: A mountain, and some very small people
cards.body: Fan Kuan painted it about 1000, in ink on a silk hanging scroll over 2 meters tall. A huge mountain fills most of the picture. The travelers are a tiny mule train near the bottom. In 1958, a scholar at the National Palace Museum in Taipei spotted Fan Kuan's signature hidden among the leaves beside the mules. The artist, too, made himself small.

cards.headline: Mountain-water
cards.body: The Chinese term for landscape painting, shan shui, means "mountain-water". Monumental landscapes like Fan Kuan's flowered in the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127). The court painter Guo Xi wrote of three distances: high, looking up at a peak; deep, peering into the valleys behind; and level, gazing across to far hills. His Early Spring of 1072 combines all three. Your eye doesn't stand still. It goes for a walk.

cards.fact: In Chinese landscapes, the mist is often just bare silk.
cards.context: Painters paid as much attention to the unpainted parts of a picture as to the painted ones. Mist and cloud are often simply silk or paper left empty, and your eye fills them with air. Remember Level 3's negative space, the empty part with a shape of its own? Here the emptiness does some of the heaviest work.

title: What Was the Renaissance?
objective: After this level you can explain what the Renaissance's rebirth meant and why it began in Florence.
summary: Florence, rich from cloth and banking, launched a rebirth of Greek and Roman learning. Its 1401 contest for bronze doors, won by Ghiberti, is often seen as the start.

cards.headline: In 1401, Florence held a contest to find its best artist.
cards.body: The prize: making bronze doors for the city's Baptistery. Seven artists entered, and each cast the same scene in bronze, Abraham about to sacrifice his son Isaac, framed in a four-lobed quatrefoil. The contest is often seen as a starting point of the Renaissance. So why here, and why then?

cards.headline: A rebirth, on purpose
cards.body: Remember Level 1? Renaissance is French for "rebirth", and what was being reborn was the learning and art of ancient Greece and Rome. It began in 14th-century Italy. Scholars called humanists pored over old Greek and Latin writings and made human nature, with all its dignity, their subject. Art still mostly served the church. You could say the Renaissance looked back to ancient Rome in order to look harder at people.

cards.fact: Florence ran on cloth and cash.
cards.context: The city grew rich making cloth and banking, and its gold coin, the florin, became a monetary standard far beyond its walls. Wealthy merchant families, the Medici above all, paid for palaces, churches and monasteries, and for the art that filled them. Art takes time and materials, and those take money. Florence had plenty.

cards.headline: The winner, and the loser
cards.body: Lorenzo Ghiberti won. His doors kept him busy from 1403 until 1424, more than two decades, and they were paid for by the Calimala, a powerful merchants' guild. The runner-up, Filippo Brunelleschi, took the loss and turned toward architecture. Keep an eye on him. He'll be back.

title: Perspective
objective: After this level you can explain how linear perspective makes a flat picture look deep.
summary: Linear perspective makes parallel lines meet at one vanishing point. Brunelleschi proved it with a peephole panel about 1415; Alberti wrote it down in 1435.

cards.headline: About 1415, Brunelleschi painted a picture with a hole in it.
cards.body: He stood just inside the doorway of Florence's unfinished cathedral and painted the Baptistery across the square on a small panel. Then he drilled a peephole through it, as small as a lentil on the painted side. The hole was part of a proof.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: parallel lines meet at a single vanishing point.

cards.headline: Lines that meet
cards.body: Stand between railway tracks and look along them. The rails never touch, yet they seem to squeeze together far away. Linear perspective turns that into a rule for pictures: all the parallel lines running away from you meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, and things get smaller as they near it. Follow the rule and a flat surface starts to look deep.

cards.headline: The peephole proof
cards.body: Here's how the test worked. You peeked through the hole from the back of the panel at a mirror held in front of it. In the mirror you saw the painted Baptistery, and you could compare it straight away with the real one, and it matched. The panel is lost now, but the method survived: in 1435, Leon Battista Alberti wrote it down in his book On Painting, so any painter could learn it.

cards.fact: A flat wall that opens into a chapel.
cards.context: Masaccio painted the Holy Trinity on a wall of Santa Maria Novella in Florence in 1425-27: Christ on the cross beneath a deep, coffered barrel vault. He drew the vault in linear perspective, so the wall seems to open into a real chapel. Level 3 called this space: the feeling of depth in a flat picture.

title: Brunelleschi's Dome
objective: After this level you can explain how Brunelleschi built Florence's great dome.
summary: Florence Cathedral waited over a century for a dome about 45 metres wide. Brunelleschi built it (1420-36) with no wooden frame, using two shells and herringbone brickwork.

cards.headline: Florence began a giant cathedral in 1296. Its dome waited over a century.
cards.body: By 1418 the building needed an eight-sided dome about 45 metres wide, and how to vault it had beaten architects for decades. The city held a contest for ideas. In 1420 it chose a goldsmith with no serious architectural training: Brunelleschi.

cards.headline: No wooden frame
cards.body: Builders normally raised an arch or dome on centering: a temporary wooden frame that holds the bricks up until the mortar sets, then comes out. Brunelleschi skipped it. From 1420 to 1436 his dome rose with no centering underneath at all, its curves kept true by a system of measuring wires.

cards.headline: Two domes and a zigzag
cards.body: Look up from inside and you see one dome, but there are two: an inner shell spanning the space and an outer shell that keeps off the weather. In the brickwork, some bricks are set at angles to the rest in a zigzag herringbone pattern. They lock each new ring of bricks to the ones below, so the dome held itself up as it grew. The wall was its own scaffolding.

cards.fact: It's still the largest masonry dome in the world.
cards.context: Nearly six centuries on, nobody has built a bigger dome of brick and stone. Brunelleschi's design for the lantern, the small tower on top, was approved in 1436, but it was finished only after his death in 1446. Not bad for the runner-up in Level 31's door contest.

title: Patrons and the Medici
objective: After this level you can explain how rich patrons like the Medici paid for Renaissance art.
summary: Renaissance art began with a patron who paid and set the terms, down to the price of ultramarine blue. The Medici, rich from banking, even had themselves painted in.

cards.headline: In 1485, a painter signed a contract that set the price of his blue.
cards.body: Domenico Ghirlandaio agreed to paint an Adoration of the Magi for Florence's foundling hospital. Like most Renaissance art, it began with a patron: the person paying for the work, who often set the pay, materials, deadline and subject in a contract.

cards.headline: Four florins an ounce
cards.body: That blue was ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli, a stone mined in north-eastern Afghanistan. It was the most expensive blue there was, so the contract named it: ultramarine at 4 florins an ounce. Ghirlandaio also had to paint the panel himself, follow an approved drawing and deliver within 30 months, for 115 florins. The patron wasn't just buying a picture. He was buying a guarantee.

cards.body: Florence's biggest patrons were the Medici, a family grown rich on cloth and banking. From 1459, Benozzo Gozzoli, chosen by Cosimo de' Medici, covered three walls of the family's palace chapel with the Procession of the Magi: riders winding through a landscape of trees and flowering meadows. Look closely at the procession. Members of the Medici family are in it.

cards.fact: Lorenzo de' Medici took a young Michelangelo into his home.
cards.context: Lorenzo, called the Magnificent, was a poet as well as a patron. Michelangelo had started out at 13 as an apprentice to Ghirlandaio, the painter with the blue contract. title: Leonardo da Vinci
objective: After this level you can describe Leonardo's paintings and his notebooks.
summary: Leonardo filled thousands of pages with mirror writing and drawings. His Mona Lisa melts light into shadow with sfumato; his experimental Last Supper began flaking in his lifetime.

cards.headline: Leonardo da Vinci wrote backwards.
cards.body: Thousands of pages of his notes survive, and they run from right to left, in mirror writing. Hold a page up to a mirror and it reads normally. Leonardo was left-handed, which made writing this way easier.

cards.headline: A notebook full of the world
cards.body: The notebooks roam across anatomy, machines and flight, and the drawings come first: the words are there to explain the pictures. Leonardo split his energy between art and science, and he finished surprisingly few paintings. You could say the notebooks were where he did his thinking, and the paintings were where he showed it.

mascot.line: One word to keep from this level: sfumato, shading that melts with no edges.

cards.headline: The smoke trick
cards.body: He began the Mona Lisa about 1503. A woman is shown half-length, turned three-quarters toward you, hands folded, with valleys and rivers winding far behind her. Now look for the edges of her smile. There aren't any. Leonardo used sfumato, from the Italian for evaporating like smoke: fine shading that lets light and dark melt into each other without lines or borders.

cards.fact: His most famous wall painting started falling apart in his lifetime.
cards.context: The Last Supper (1495-98) covers a dining-hall wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan: Christ has just said that one of the apostles will betray him, and they react. Instead of true fresco on wet plaster, Leonardo painted in tempera on a dry wall. It was an experiment, and it was already deteriorating while he was alive.

title: Michelangelo
objective: After this level you can describe the David and the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
summary: Michelangelo carved the David (1501-04) from an abandoned block, showing David before the fight. A sculptor at heart, he then painted the Sistine ceiling standing up.

cards.headline: Florence owned a giant block of marble that nobody could use.
cards.body: Two earlier sculptors had started on it and rejected it for its flaws, and it lay abandoned for about 25 years. In 1501 the job went to a 26-year-old named Michelangelo.

cards.headline: David, before the fight
cards.body: By 1504 the block had become a marble nude 5.17 metres tall: weight on one leg, a sling so slim you can barely see it, watchful eyes. Earlier Florentine artists showed David triumphant over Goliath. Michelangelo's is usually read as David before the battle, concentrating. A committee that included Leonardo set him up in Florence's main square as a symbol of the republic's liberty.

cards.headline: A sculptor on a ceiling
cards.body: Pope Julius II then put him to work on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. Michelangelo thought of himself as a sculptor, and he'd never painted a fresco. He did it anyway, from 1508 to 1512, standing upright on scaffolding he designed himself. The famous picture of him lying on his back is a myth, probably from a 1965 film.

cards.fact: In the Creation of Adam, two fingers almost touch.
cards.context: Nine scenes from Genesis run down the middle of the ceiling. In the Creation of Adam, Adam lounges on the ground and lifts a limp hand, while God, carried by angels in swirling drapery, reaches toward him. Their fingertips nearly meet, but not quite. All the drama lives in that sliver of empty space.

title: Raphael and the High Renaissance
objective: After this level you can explain what made High Renaissance painting feel balanced and calm.
summary: Raphael's School of Athens puts Plato and Aristotle at its vanishing point. High Renaissance paintings like his Madonna in the Meadow build calm from balance and triangles.

cards.headline: In one room of the Vatican, the great thinkers of ancient Greece meet.
cards.body: Raphael painted them there on a single wall about 1509-11, while Michelangelo was painting the Sistine ceiling nearby. Two of the Renaissance's biggest names, working a short walk apart.

cards.headline: Who's who
cards.body: The School of Athens sets the philosophers in a vast hall of arches and barrel vaults, said to be based on Bramante's design for the new St. Peter's. At the center stand Plato, pointing up to the sky, and Aristotle, gesturing down toward the earth. Leaning on a block of marble in front is Heraclitus, a portrait of Michelangelo. And at the far right, in a black beret, is Raphael himself.

cards.headline: Every line leads to the middle
cards.body: Now follow the lines of the architecture inward. They meet at the painting's central vanishing point, and that's exactly where Plato and Aristotle stand. Level 32's rule is doing the pointing: wherever your eye starts, the building steers it to the two main characters.

cards.fact: High Renaissance painting aims for perfect balance.
cards.context: The Renaissance hit its height between the 1490s and the 1520s, the High Renaissance. In Raphael's Madonna in the Meadow (1505/06), Mary sits on the ground with the baby Jesus and the young John the Baptist, and the three fit inside an equilateral triangle. Wide at the base, peaked at the top: nothing wobbles. Raphael died at 37, in 1520, yet for centuries he was seen as the supreme High Renaissance painter.

summary: Woodcuts print from raised wood; engravings from lines cut in metal. One block prints again and again, so Dürer's images, even his armored rhino, traveled all over Europe.

cards.body: An Indian rhinoceros had arrived in Lisbon. Albrecht Dürer, a German artist, worked from a letter describing it and a sketch by someone who had seen it. Then he made a picture that could be printed over and over.

cards.headline: One design, many pictures
cards.body: Once a block or plate is ready, it can print the same picture over and over with little loss of detail. Words already traveled this way: Gutenberg's press, which printed his Bible around 1455, made books cheap to produce in large numbers. Pictures rode along. Dürer studied Italian engravings on a trip to Italy in 1494-95, and his Apocalypse woodcuts of 1498 made him famous, even back in Italy. A painting stays on its wall. A print travels.

It was wrong, but it was printed and copied into natural history books, and it stayed Europe's standard rhinoceros until a touring rhino called Clara became a sensation in the 1700s. That's the power of a print: a mistake can travel too.

He told art's story in three acts: ancient greatness, medieval decline, then a rinascita, a rebirth, starting in 14th-century Tuscany and peaking with Michelangelo. title: Baroque Drama
objective: After this level you can explain how Baroque art used movement and emotion to grab the viewer.
summary: Baroque, named after a misshapen pearl, began in Italy around 1600. The Church wanted art that stirred faith, so artists used diagonals, motion and illusion, like Rubens's cross and Pozzo's fake dome.

cards.headline: Baroque started out as an insult. It probably means a lumpy pearl.
cards.body: The word likely comes from barroco, Portuguese for an irregularly shaped pearl, and for centuries critics used it to mean odd and overdone. The art it names began in Italy in the late 1500s and filled the 1600s. It aimed for drama, movement and emotion. It wanted to grab you.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: Baroque drama had a job, to stir the faith of ordinary people.

cards.headline: The Church wanted art that moved you
cards.body: After the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563), the Catholic Church gave art a job: strengthen ordinary people's faith. The pictures had to be clear and lifelike, so anyone could read them without a scholar standing by. And they had to use dramatic effects that stirred real feeling. A calm, clever puzzle for experts would not do. The Church wanted art that hit you in the chest.

cards.fact: Rubens caught the cross halfway up.
cards.context: In The Elevation of the Cross (about 1610), painted for Antwerp's cathedral, muscular men strain to heave the cross upright. It cuts across the picture on a steep diagonal, stuck between lying down and standing. You arrive mid-heave, while the effort is still going on. Stormy diagonals and full-blooded bodies like these are seen as the essence of Baroque painting.

cards.headline: A dome that isn't there
cards.body: Walk into the church of Sant'Ignazio in Rome and look up: a dome rises over you. It's paint. In 1685 Andrea Pozzo painted it on a flat surface, because the Jesuits had apparently run out of money for a real one. A disc set in the floor marks the one spot where the illusion works. Step off it and the dome gives itself away.

title: Caravaggio and Light
objective: After this level you can explain chiaroscuro and Caravaggio's dramatic lighting.
summary: Chiaroscuro means light-dark. Caravaggio pushed it to tenebrism, letting a beam of light tell the story in The Calling of Saint Matthew, with saints modeled on ordinary people.

cards.headline: In a dark chapel in Rome, a beam of light walks into a room full of tax men.
cards.body: Around 1600, Caravaggio painted Christ pointing at a man counting coins at a table. He barely needed a caption, because the light tells you where to look. To see how, you need one Italian word.

mascot.line: Easy to mix up: chiaroscuro is light and shadow for solidity; tenebrism is its harshest version.

cards.fact: Chiaroscuro means light-dark.
cards.context: It's Italian: chiaro, light, and scuro, dark. It means using light and shadow to make things look solid. Hold a flashlight beside your face in a dark room and you'll see it. Caravaggio pushed it to the edge. That harshest version is called tenebrism: a hard light picks figures out of deep darkness, and everything else disappears.

cards.headline: The light does the pointing
cards.body: In The Calling of Saint Matthew, men in the clothes of Caravaggio's own day sit counting coins at a table. At the right, Christ steps in and points. A beam of light crosses the dark room to the faces at the table, pointing at Matthew just as Christ's hand does. One man points to himself, as if to ask: me? Your eye follows the light to the answer.

cards.headline: Saints with dirty feet
cards.body: Caravaggio painted holy figures from ordinary people off the street, in ragged clothes and with dirty feet. Some viewers pushed back, since they were used to elegant, graceful saints. But his hard light and real faces caught on. Among the painters he influenced are two you'll meet soon in this chapter: Rembrandt and Velázquez.

summary: Bernini froze marble mid-action: David about to throw, with you in Goliath's place, and Daphne turning into a tree. His colonnades at St. Peter's wrap the square like arms.

cards.headline: Stand in front of Bernini's David, and you're Goliath.
cards.body: Bernini carved David in the instant before he hurls the stone, and he meant the viewer to stand where the giant would be. The sculpture isn't just in the room with you. It's aiming at you.

cards.headline: A hero caught mid-throw
cards.body: Bernini's marble David (1623 to 1624) twists like a coiled spring, arms tense on the sling, the stone about to fly. You get the split second before the action, not a pose after it. There's a personal touch too: according to early sources, David's face is Bernini's own. Standing in Goliath's spot, you're looking at the sculptor's determination.

cards.fact: Bernini made marble turn into a tree.
cards.context: In Apollo and Daphne (1622 to 1625), the god Apollo finally reaches the nymph he's chasing, and she's already changing into a laurel tree. Roots grow from her feet. Leaves sprout from her fingers. Where Apollo's hand lands, there's bark. It's one block of stone, caught in the middle of becoming something else.

cards.headline: A square that hugs you
cards.body: Bernini also designed the colonnades of St. Peter's Square in Rome (1656 to 1667): 284 columns in four rows, curving around the square. They symbolize the Church's arms embracing the faithful. And there's a trick. From either of two marble discs in the pavement, the four rows line up and look like one. Remember Pozzo's disc in Level 41? Baroque Rome loved a sweet spot.

cards.headline: A group photo that won't stand still
cards.body: Group portraits usually lined people up in stiff rows, like a team photo. Rembrandt made the company move. The captain, in black with a red sash, strides forward beside his lieutenant in pale cream. Behind them glows a girl in yellow, the company's mascot. Strong chiaroscuro spotlights some figures and sinks others into shadow, like actors on a stage.

cards.fact: About 80 Rembrandt self-portraits survive.
cards.context: They span a 40-year career in paintings, etchings and drawings, far more than any other painter of his time. Scroll through them and you watch a man age.

cards.headline: Why so many? Several good guesses

title: The Dutch Golden Age
objective: After this level you can explain why Dutch painters sold everyday scenes and still lifes.
summary: Dutch Calvinist churches banned images, so painters sold on an open market instead: over a million paintings, some cheaper than linen, and specialists like Heda painting still lifes.

cards.headline: In 1640, a visitor found paintings in the blacksmith's shop.
cards.body: The English traveller Peter Mundy wrote that in Amsterdam even blacksmiths and cobblers kept a picture by their forge or in their stall. Elsewhere in Europe, paintings mostly hung in churches and palaces. Why were Dutch paintings everywhere?

mascot.line: This is the cause behind the whole level: no church customers, so painters sold on an open market.

cards.headline: The church was closed for business
cards.body: In the Dutch Republic, Calvinist teaching banned images in churches, though not in homes or town halls. That removed the customer that Level 41's Rubens painted for. Elsewhere, artists could hope for big commissions from the church or the state. Dutch painters had a growing independent art market instead: they painted first and found a buyer after.

cards.fact: An estimated 1.3 to 1.4 million paintings were made in 20 years.
cards.context: That's in the Netherlands from 1640 to 1659, for a population of about 2 million. Some oil paintings cost less than household linen or a piece of furniture, so ordinary families could hang them. Picture a country with more new paintings than half its people.

cards.headline: Pick a lane, own it
cards.body: With so many painters selling, many specialized in one subject, like landscape or still life, to build a reputation and a profitable niche. Willem Claesz. Heda of Haarlem was a still-life man. In 1634 he painted oysters, a lemon, a tall glass and a silver bowl on a table, full of gleaming reflections. Buyers knew exactly what a Heda was.

title: Vermeer
objective: After this level you can describe Vermeer's quiet interiors and how he painted light.
summary: Only about 36 Vermeers survive. In The Milkmaid, window light falls on a still kitchen, built from hundreds of colored dots. Whether he used a camera obscura is still debated.

cards.headline: Only about 36 paintings by Vermeer survive.
cards.body: He worked in Delft, and outside his region he was little known until the 1800s, when the critic Théophile Thoré brought him international fame. So what makes so few quiet pictures so famous? Mostly one thing: the light.

cards.headline: The loudest thing is the milk
cards.body: In The Milkmaid (about 1660), a maid stands at a table and pours milk from a jug into a bowl. Bread sits beside her. Daylight falls through a window on the left and fills the small kitchen. Except for the thin stream of milk, everything is still. No drama, no saints, no crowd. Just someone doing a chore, and doing it with total care.

cards.fact: Vermeer built light out of dots.
cards.context: Look closely at The Milkmaid and the light on the bread and the jug breaks into hundreds of small colored dots of paint. Some are blurred little spots, like the sparkle in an out-of-focus photo. Step back and they turn into crust catching the sun.

cards.headline: Did he use a camera?
cards.body: Those blurred light spots match what you see in a camera obscura, a device that projects an image through a lens. So some think Vermeer used one. But no document from his time shows he owned or used a camera obscura. It stays a debated idea, a good guess with no receipt.

title: Velázquez
objective: After this level you can explain why Las Meninas still puzzles viewers.
summary: Las Meninas (1656) shows the young infanta, her maids of honor and Velázquez at a huge hidden canvas. A mirror reflects the king and queen, so what is he painting, and where are you standing?

cards.headline: Centuries later, nobody agrees what this painting is of.
cards.body: It's Las Meninas, painted in 1656 by Diego Velázquez, painter to the king of Spain. It looks like a simple scene at court. Then you notice the mirror.

cards.headline: A princess and her court
cards.body: At the center stands the five-year-old Infanta Margarita Teresa, the king's daughter. Her maids of honor, the meninas, attend her. Nearby are two people with dwarfism and a big dog lying on the floor. It could be an ordinary afternoon in the palace. Almost.

cards.headline: The painter is in the painting
cards.body: From 1623 Velázquez worked for King Philip IV, the only painter allowed to paint the king. In Las Meninas he put himself in the scene: at the left, brush in hand, in front of a huge canvas. We see only its back. Whatever he's painting, we're not allowed to look.

cards.fact: The mirror shows the king and queen.
cards.context: On the back wall, a small mirror reflects King Philip IV and Queen Mariana. So where are they? One reading says they stand where you stand, and everyone has just noticed them. Another says the mirror shows the hidden canvas. The painting leaves it open, which is why it's often called a painting about painting.

title: Rococo
objective: After this level you can describe the playful, pastel Rococo style.
summary: Rococo began in early-1700s Paris as a lighter answer to Louis XIV's heavy Baroque: shell-like curves, pastels and flirtation. Fragonard's The Swing, with its flying slipper, is its signature.

cards.headline: A pink dress, a swing, and a slipper flying through the air.
cards.body: In Fragonard's The Swing (about 1767 to 1768), a young woman flies up in pink silk. An older man pushes the swing. Down in the bushes, a young lover gazes up. One of her slippers has just kicked off into the air. Welcome to the Rococo.

cards.headline: From grand to cozy
cards.body: Rococo began in Paris in the early 1700s as a reaction against the heavy Baroque of Louis XIV's reign. Think of a switch from a cathedral organ to a harpsichord. It flourished from about 1700 to 1770, filling paintings with myth and courtship instead of saints and struggle.

mascot.line: Easy to mix up. Baroque: the lumpy pearl. Rococo: the grotto seashells.

cards.fact: Rococo is named after grotto seashells.
cards.context: The word comes from the French rocaille, the shell-covered rockwork used to decorate artificial grottoes. The style loved curling C and S shapes, light pastels, ivory white and gold, and lighthearted scenes of myth and courtship. If Baroque shouts, Rococo flirts.

cards.headline: The Swing's cheeky backstory
cards.body: According to an account from 1767, a gentleman of the court first asked the painter Doyen for a picture of his mistress on a swing pushed by a bishop, with himself admiring her legs. Doyen refused and passed the job to Fragonard. By then, critics were already attacking Rococo as frivolous, and a stricter style would soon replace it in France.
