title: Neoclassicism
objective: After this level you can explain why artists turned back to Greece and Rome in the late 1700s.
summary: Digging up Herculaneum and Pompeii and Winckelmann's praise of Greek 'noble simplicity' turned artists from Rococo to Greece and Rome. David's Oath of the Horatii (1784) became the style's manifesto.

cards.headline: In 1748, diggers began uncovering a Roman city frozen in time.
cards.body: Mount Vesuvius had buried Pompeii under ash and pumice in 79 CE. Excavations at nearby Herculaneum had begun in 1738, and at Pompeii in 1748. A Roman city came back into the light, and artists took note. Neoclassicism, peaking in the 1780s and 1790s, turned against the Rococo and back toward the ancient world.

cards.fact: Noble simplicity and quiet grandeur.
cards.context: That's how the scholar Johann Joachim Winckelmann described Greek art, and he urged artists to imitate it. After decades of Rococo swings and slippers, the idea landed like a glass of cold water: less frill, more calm.

cards.headline: Three brothers, three swords
cards.body: In Jacques-Louis David's Oath of the Horatii (1784), three Roman brothers stand in a row and stretch out their arms to swear an oath before their father, who holds up their swords. They will fight for Rome. To the side, the women of the family slump in grief. David used firm outlines, bare space, sober color and clear light, with the figures lined up like a carved frieze.

cards.headline: Straight lines after all those curves
cards.body: Neoclassical painting preferred line over color and straight lines over curves. Put the Oath next to The Swing and you can see the turn. Shown in Paris in 1785, the Oath caused a sensation as a manifesto for reviving art. Later it was read as a call for stern, patriotic, republican morals. Same painting, new meaning.

title: Romanticism
objective: After this level you can explain how Romantic artists painted storms, feeling and the sublime.
summary: Romantics put feeling before reason. Friedrich's Wanderer faces the sublime, Burke's mix of awe and terror; Géricault painted a real shipwreck on a canvas about 5 by 7 meters.

cards.headline: A man stands on a rocky peak, his back to you, staring into a sea of fog.
cards.body: Caspar David Friedrich finished him about 1817. You never see his face, so you end up looking where he looks: out over ridges and mountaintops poking up through the mist. Seeing a figure from behind like this invites you to share his view. Welcome to Romanticism.

cards.headline: Feeling beats reason
cards.body: From the late 1700s to the mid-1800s, Romantic artists put emotion, imagination and the individual first. It was partly a reaction against the Enlightenment's trust in reason and order, and against calm Neoclassical art. Friedrich said a painter should paint not only what is in front of him but also what he sees inside himself. So the Wanderer isn't a postcard of one real view: Friedrich stitched it together from sketches of several places.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Beautiful is small and smooth; sublime is vast and a little frightening.

cards.fact: Romantic painters wanted a view that scares you, a little.
cards.context: In 1757 the writer Edmund Burke split two feelings apart. The beautiful is small, smooth and delicate. The sublime is vast, rugged and powerful, and it stirs awe mixed with terror. A daisy is beautiful; a cliff edge in a gale is sublime. Friedrich's Wanderer is often read as an image of exactly that: the sublime power of nature.

cards.headline: A shipwreck the size of a wall
cards.body: In 1816 the French frigate Medusa ran aground off West Africa. About 150 people were set adrift on a raft; after 13 days, only 15 were alive. Théodore Géricault chose that recent, real disaster over an ancient hero. After meeting survivors and building a scale model of the raft, he painted it in 1818-19, about 5 by 7 meters. Bodies pile into a pyramid rising to a man waving a cloth at a tiny ship on the horizon. At the 1819 Salon, some critics were captivated and others repulsed.

title: Goya
objective: After this level you can describe Goya's path from court painter to dark visions.
summary: Goya became Spain's first court painter, went deaf in 1792, attacked abuses in Los Caprichos, painted The Third of May 1808 and covered his own walls with the Black Paintings.

cards.headline: Spain's top court painter ended up painting nightmares on his own walls.
cards.body: Francisco Goya painted for the king of Spain. Near the end of his life, one of his pictures showed the god Saturn devouring one of his own children. How do you get from the palace to that?

cards.headline: The king's painter goes deaf
cards.body: Goya climbed fast: painter to the king in 1786, first court painter in 1799. But an illness in 1792 left him permanently deaf, and afterward his work turned darker and more critical. In 1799 he published Los Caprichos, 80 etchings attacking political, social and religious abuses. In one, The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters, the artist sleeps at his desk while owls and bats swarm around him. The set was withdrawn from sale after a few days.

cards.headline: The Third of May 1808
cards.body: In 1808, during Napoleon's occupation of Spain, French troops executed Spanish insurgents in Madrid. Goya painted it in 1814. A lantern lights one man in a white shirt, arms flung up in a Christlike pose, marks like stigmata on his palms. Facing him is the firing squad: a faceless, uniform row. The victims are individual people; the soldiers could be anyone.

cards.fact: Goya's darkest paintings were painted on the walls of his own house.
cards.context: Between about 1819 and 1823, Goya painted 14 dark murals, now called the Black Paintings, straight onto the walls of his house outside Madrid, the Quinta del Sordo. In one, a wild-eyed Saturn devours one of his children. A new owner bought the house in 1873 and had the murals transferred to canvas. They hang in the Prado today.

title: Landscape Painting
objective: After this level you can explain how Turner and Constable made landscape a serious subject.
summary: Academies ranked landscape near the bottom. Constable studied his home valley and its skies; Turner painted storms and speed. The Hay Wain won gold in Paris in 1824.

cards.headline: In 1824, a painting of a hay cart in a river won a gold medal in Paris.
cards.body: It was The Hay Wain by the Englishman John Constable, and it had failed to sell when shown in London. It won the medal at the Paris Salon, from King Charles X himself. Not bad for a picture with no heroes in it, in an age when landscape was supposed to be minor art.

cards.headline: Painting's pecking order
cards.body: The French Royal Academy ranked what you could paint. History painting came first, then portraits, then everyday scenes, and only then landscape and still life. History ranked highest because it showed noble events of history and religion. Landscape sat near the bottom because it had no human subject: a view of a field, however lovely, was officially minor art.

cards.headline: Constable reads the sky
cards.body: Constable, born in East Bergholt in Suffolk, painted the Stour valley where he grew up. The Hay Wain (1821) shows an empty hay wagon crossing the shallow millpond at Flatford. He painted it in his London studio, working from outdoor sketches made over several years. And he studied the sky: on Hampstead Heath in 1821 and 1822 he painted dozens of cloud studies, "skying", noting the date, time and wind on the back of each.

cards.headline: Turner paints the weather itself
cards.body: J.M.W. Turner went further. In Snow Storm (about 1842), a steamboat is tossed in a swirling vortex where water and light merge. Turner claimed he had himself lashed to a ship's mast for four hours to watch the storm; historians doubt it. Some critics sneered "soapsuds and whitewash". In Rain, Steam and Speed (1844), a steam train rushes straight at you across a bridge through the rain.

title: Realism
objective: After this level you can explain why Realists painted ordinary workers instead of heroes.
summary: Realism (about 1850-80) showed ordinary life plainly. Courbet painted a village funeral at history-painting size; Millet's Gleaners gave poor women a grandeur that alarmed the wealthy.

cards.headline: At the Salon of 1850-51: a village funeral, about 7 meters wide.
cards.body: Gustave Courbet's A Burial at Ornans shows more than 40 life-size people at a funeral in his small hometown. There are no angels and no heaven opening up: just mourners around a hole in the ground. Salon visitors were perplexed by its size and its ordinary subject.

cards.headline: What Realism meant
cards.body: Realism, a French movement from about 1850 to 1880, set out to show contemporary life accurately, without prettying it up, especially ordinary and humble people. Realists rejected both the classical and the Romantic styles taught by the academies. Courbet was the first to proclaim it openly as a program. And the size was part of the argument: canvases that huge were traditionally reserved for history and religious painting.

cards.headline: The Stone Breakers
cards.body: In 1849 Courbet painted two men breaking stones by a road, one young and one old. That was the whole subject, and the frank plainness of it shocked public and critics. You can only see it in photographs now: the painting was destroyed in the bombing of Dresden in February 1945.

cards.fact: Three women picking up scraps made the rich nervous.
cards.context: In Millet's The Gleaners (1857), three peasant women bend low over a field, gathering the stray stalks of grain left after the harvest, an old right of the rural poor. Behind them, far away, sit huge grain stacks and a heavily loaded wagon. Millet gave peasant laborers a grandeur once reserved for important people. Shown less than ten years after the revolution of 1848, the picture was read by many comfortable viewers as a threat.

title: Photography Arrives
objective: After this level you can explain how photography changed what painters thought painting was for.
summary: Niépce's first photo took hours or days; Daguerre's 1839 process took minutes. Cameras recorded the world exactly, and Muybridge proved painters had drawn galloping horses wrong.

cards.headline: Possibly the first photo of a person: a man getting his boots shined.
cards.body: About 1838, Louis Daguerre photographed a busy Paris street, the Boulevard du Temple. The exposure was so long that every moving carriage and walker vanished. Only a man standing still for a shoeshine stayed put long enough to appear.

cards.headline: Minutes instead of days
cards.body: The oldest surviving camera photograph, made by Nicéphore Niépce in 1826 or 1827, needed hours of light, perhaps days. Daguerre, once Niépce's partner, found a much faster process. On January 9, 1839, it was announced at the Academy of Sciences in Paris: the daguerreotype. Each one was a one-of-a-kind image on a polished, silver-plated copper plate, with no negative to print copies from.

mascot.line: This is Level 1's idea again: once a machine could copy the world, painting no longer had to.

cards.fact: "From today, painting is dead."
cards.context: That's what the painter Paul Delaroche is reported to have said on seeing the daguerreotype. Painting survived, but Level 1 told you what really changed: photography freed painting from being the only way to show the world accurately. If a machine can copy a street, a painter has to ask what else painting is for.

cards.headline: The camera catches the horse
cards.body: Painters long showed a galloping horse in a "flying gallop", legs stretched out front and back, as in Géricault's Epsom Derby of 1821. In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge, hired by the railroad magnate Leland Stanford, photographed a galloping horse with a row of cameras. The horse does lift all four hooves off the ground, but with its legs tucked under its body, not stretched out. Some people refused to believe a horse could look like that.

title: Impressionism
objective: After this level you can explain how the Impressionists painted light and passing moments outdoors.
summary: Shut out of the Salon, painters held their own show in 1874; a critic mocking Impression, Sunrise named them. They painted outdoors in dabs of pure color, with colored shadows.

cards.headline: Impressionism got its name from an insult.
cards.body: In April 1874, painters rejected by the official Salon held their own exhibition in Paris, in the photographer Nadar's former studio. A critic, Louis Leroy, picked on one picture's title to mock them all as "impressionists". The name stuck.

cards.headline: The picture that named a movement
cards.body: It was Claude Monet's Impression, Sunrise (1872): the harbor at Le Havre in the early morning. Cranes, masts and smokestacks blur together; rowboats sit in the water; a small orange sun hangs above, its reflection streaked across the waves. Leroy wrote that wallpaper in its early stages was more finished. Monet wasn't after finish. He was after light at one moment.

mascot.line: Treat the paint-tube story with care. Painters had been working outdoors for decades.

cards.headline: Out of the studio
cards.body: Painters had usually finished landscapes in the studio, from sketches. Impressionists such as Monet painted entirely outdoors, in front of the scene, trying to record colors as they appeared in natural light at a given moment. It's often said that paint tubes made this possible: in 1841 the American John Goffe Rand patented a squeezable tin tube, and before that, paint was stored in pig bladders. But painters had worked outdoors for decades, with portable easels and paint boxes too.

cards.headline: Dabs of color, colored shadows
cards.body: Get close to an Impressionist painting and it breaks into flecks and dabs of pure color, placed side by side. They also stopped using gray and black for shadows and painted them with complementary colors instead. Remember Chevreul in Level 4? Complements side by side make each other look more intense, and his ideas influenced the Impressionists.

cards.headline: Claude Monet painted the same stacks of grain 25 times. On purpose.
cards.body: Between late summer 1890 and February 1891, in a field near his home at Giverny, Monet kept going back to the same few grainstacks. The stacks hardly change. Everything around them does.

cards.headline: The real subject is the light
cards.body: Each canvas catches different light, weather and season: end of summer, snow, sunset. Monet worked on several at once, switching canvases as the light changed. In May 1891 he showed 15 of them at his dealer's gallery in Paris, to acclaim. They were his first series: pictures meant to be seen together, so you can watch the light change from one to the next.

cards.headline: A cathedral, about 30 times
cards.body: Then he did it to a building. In 1892 and 1893 Monet painted the front of Rouen Cathedral about 30 times, from rooms across the square, switching canvases as the light moved through the day. The carved stone never moves. The light does all the work.

cards.fact: Monet's last series surrounds you.
cards.context: Monet moved to Giverny in 1883 and created a water-lily pond there. It became his final subject: the Water Lilies, almost 300 paintings, more than 40 of them very large. The day after the 1918 Armistice he offered panels to France. In 1927, months after his death, they were hung in two oval rooms at the Orangerie in Paris. He wanted "the illusion of an endless whole, of a wave with no horizon and no shore."

title: Degas and Modern Life
objective: After this level you can describe how Degas captured dancers and city life.
summary: Degas, who preferred to be called a realist, painted dancers backstage and in rehearsal, cafés from off-center angles, and shocked Paris with a wax dancer in a real tutu.

cards.headline: In 1881, Edgar Degas showed a wax girl in a real tutu. People were outraged.
cards.body: Little Dancer Aged Fourteen was modeled on Marie van Goethem, a student of the Paris Opera ballet. She wore a real tulle tutu and a silk hair ribbon, with a wig of real hair. Viewers used to idealized women carved in marble didn't know what to do with her.

cards.headline: The painter of dancers
cards.body: At least half of Degas's mature work is about dance: about 1,500 paintings, pastels, prints and drawings. Few show a performance. Degas went to classes, rehearsals and the wings of the Paris Opera. His dim rehearsal rooms and gaslit stages set him apart from Monet and Pissarro, who responded to sunlight. They chased the sun; Degas chased the gas lamps.

cards.headline: An Impressionist who hated the name
cards.body: Degas helped organize the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874, yet he disliked the name and preferred to call himself a realist. He scorned painting landscapes outdoors and worked in the studio from drawings. What made him modern was how he looked at Paris: extreme viewpoints and radical perspective.

cards.fact: In a Paris café, two people sit side by side, alone together.
cards.context: In L'Absinthe (1875-76), a woman stares blankly at a glass of absinthe next to a man in a hat who looks away. Degas pushed the pair off-center and left a large, empty foreground of café tables, so you seem to glance at them from across the room. His models were the actress Ellen Andrée and the artist Marcellin Desboutin. Critics called it disgusting.

cards.body: Her name was Berthe Morisot, and she was one of the founding Impressionists. She, and the American Mary Cassatt, painted modern life too, but a different part of it.

cards.headline: Morisot: private moments
cards.body: Morisot showed in all but one of the eight Impressionist exhibitions, missing 1879, just after her daughter Julie was born. At the first, in 1874, she hung The Cradle (1872): her sister Edma watches her sleeping baby through the cradle's thin curtain. Morisot painted mainly women and children, indoors, in gardens and in parks near her home, with quick brushstrokes.

cards.headline: Cassatt: the American in Paris

That same year Degas visited her studio and invited her to exhibit with the Impressionists, and she first did so in 1879, the only American officially in the group. Degas even worked on the background of her Little Girl in a Blue Armchair (1878), in which a child sprawls across a big armchair.

cards.headline: Why these rooms?
cards.body: Cassatt's The Child's Bath (1893) looks down from above at a woman washing a child's feet in a basin, their heads touching. Why so many mothers, children and drawing rooms? Social rules of the time limited where a respectable woman could go and whom she could paint. Cassatt and Morisot turned to family, friends and private spaces, and found their subjects there.

title: Checkpoint: Revolutions in Art
objective: After this level you can trace art from Romanticism through Realism to Impressionism.
summary: The official Salon's jury decided what Paris saw. Courbet built his own pavilion, Napoleon III allowed a show of rejects in 1863, and in 1874 the Impressionists went independent.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: who decided which paintings Paris got to see?
cards.body: For more than a century, a jury did: the official Salon's. Again and again in this chapter, artists ran into it, then found ways around it. First, the chapter in order.

cards.headline: The jury and its rebels
cards.body: The Salon was France's official art show, sponsored by the government. It began in 1667, became annual after 1737, and from 1748 a jury chose what went on the walls. Rebels found ways around it. In 1855, after the Paris world's fair rejected his huge painting The Studio, Courbet showed it in his own pavilion labeled "Realism". In 1863 Emperor Napoleon III ordered a Salon des Refusés for works the jury had rejected; Manet's Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe caused a scandal there.

cards.fact: In 1874, the rejected stopped asking.
cards.context: Consistently turned away by the Salon, the Impressionists held their own exhibition in 1874 and seven more after it, up to 1886. After 1881, as independent exhibitions grew more important, the Salon gradually lost its influence and prestige. The revolution wasn't only in how paintings looked. It was also in who got to decide where they hung.

title: Post-Impressionism
objective: After this level you can explain how Cézanne, Gauguin and Seurat pushed past Impressionism.
summary: In 1910 Roger Fry named the Post-Impressionists, painters who each took Impressionism a different way: Cézanne toward solid structure, Gauguin toward imagined color, Seurat toward color science.

cards.headline: In 1910, a London critic needed one name for painters who agreed on nothing.
cards.body: Roger Fry was staging a show called Manet and the Post-Impressionists. His label is famously vague: "post" just means "after". It had to be. Cézanne, Gauguin, Seurat and Van Gogh had each taken Impressionism somewhere different. Here are three of those roads.

cards.headline: Cézanne: find the solid underneath
cards.body: The Impressionists painted the play of light. Paul Cézanne moved away from those effects and went after what lies underneath: the structure of natural forms. In a 1904 letter to the painter Émile Bernard, he gave his famous advice: treat nature by the cylinder, the sphere and the cone. A tree trunk is a cylinder, an apple a sphere, a mountain a cone. It sounds like a geometry lesson, and in a way it was.

cards.headline: Gauguin: paint what they imagine
cards.body: Paul Gauguin's Vision of the Sermon (1888) is split by a tree. On one side, praying Breton women in crisp white bonnets. On the other, Jacob wrestles an angel on a field of flat red. No meadow looks like that, and it isn't meant to: Gauguin used pure, flat color and heavy outlines, and turned away from painting straight from nature. He wrote that the landscape and the fight exist only in the imagination of the people praying. The red is the vision.

cards.fact: One label, three roads: structure, imagination and science.
cards.context: Georges Seurat took the third road. He tried to put Impressionism's light and color on a scientific basis, with tiny dots of color set side by side (Level 63 zooms in). So Post-Impressionism isn't one style. It's a family of very different painters, each answering Impressionism in their own way.

title: Van Gogh
objective: After this level you can describe Van Gogh's brushwork, his colors and his life.
summary: Van Gogh made some 900 paintings in about ten years and sold little. He painted The Starry Night from memory in 1889, in thick impasto, and used red and green to express feeling.

cards.headline: About ten years of painting. Some 900 paintings. He sold little of it.
cards.body: Vincent van Gogh painted from 1880 to 1890, and alongside those 900 paintings he made about 1,100 drawings. Yet he sold little of his art while he was alive. One of those paintings is a night sky you have almost certainly seen. Here's how he made it.

cards.headline: The Starry Night, painted from memory
cards.body: In 1889 Van Gogh was a patient at an asylum near Saint-Rémy, in southern France. He could watch the sky from his barred bedroom window, but he couldn't paint in that room, so he painted it from memory or drawings. Picture it: a sky churning with blue swirls, a yellow crescent moon, stars like glowing orbs. A dark cypress rises on the left like a flame, and below, a small village glows with yellow windows.

cards.headline: Paint you could run a finger over
cards.body: For The Starry Night he squeezed paint straight from the tube onto the canvas. The result is impasto: paint laid on so thickly that it stands up in ridges, and every stroke keeps its shape. The swirls in that sky aren't just drawn; they're built, stroke by stroke, like frosting on a cake.

mascot.line: Hold on to this: color for feeling. It's the heart of Level 65's Expressionism.

cards.fact: Van Gogh used color to carry feelings, not just to copy what he saw.
cards.context: In 1888 he painted The Night Café and wrote to his brother Theo that he'd tried to express the terrible human passions with the red and the green. The room is blood-red; the billiard table is green. Everywhere, he wrote, it's a battle of greens and reds. He wasn't reporting the decor. He was making the room feel like a fight.

title: Seurat and Pointillism
objective: After this level you can explain how dots of pure color blend in the eye.
summary: Seurat built La Grande Jatte from tiny strokes of pure color that blend in the viewer's eye: pointillism, shaped by Chevreul's color theories.

cards.headline: Up close, it's confetti. Step back, and it's a Sunday afternoon.
cards.body: Georges Seurat spent about two years on one giant painting made of tiny touches of color. Walk up to it and the people dissolve into specks. Walk away and they come back. The mixing doesn't happen on the canvas. It happens in your eye.

cards.headline: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
cards.body: Seurat painted it in 1884–86. Parisians spend a Sunday afternoon on the Grande Jatte, an island in the Seine: some stroll along the river, some picnic on the grass. The canvas is huge, about 2 by 3 meters, wider than most sofas are long. And every inch of it is built from tiny, separate strokes of pure color, too small to pick out when you take in the whole picture.

cards.headline: Mixing in the eye, not on the palette
cards.body: That's pointillism: small dots or strokes of color placed side by side, so that from a distance they blend together. Why not just mix the paint first? Remember Level 4: mix complements as paint and they cancel into brown. Seurat kept his colors pure and separate, and let your eye do the mixing. The result seems to shimmer.
cards.callout: Paint mixed on the palette gets duller. Colors mixed in the eye stay bright.

cards.fact: Seurat met Level 4's color scientist, Chevreul, in person.

Seurat experimented with his theories. He called his own method chromo-luminarism. Everyone else settled on pointillism (it's also called divisionism).

title: Art Nouveau
objective: After this level you can describe Art Nouveau's flowing lines and plant forms.
summary: Art Nouveau (about 1890 to 1910) was a deliberate new style of plant-like, whiplash lines, seen in Guimard's Paris Métro entrances, glass, jewelry and posters.

cards.headline: In Paris, you can still go down into the subway through an iron garden.
cards.body: From 1900, Hector Guimard designed entrances for the new Paris Métro in cast iron and glass. Stems of green-painted iron curl up into lamps shaped like flower buds, under a sign reading Métropolitain. It was a new style for a new century, and it had a name that said so.

cards.headline: The line that never goes straight
cards.body: Art Nouveau flourished from about 1890 to 1910, across Europe and the US. Its signature is an undulating, lopsided line, like a flower stalk, a curling vine tendril or the edge of an insect's wing. At its most energetic it snaps with a whiplike force. Once you know it, you'll spot it curling through old railings, windows and posters.

cards.headline: Art moves out of the frame
cards.body: Painting wasn't the main event. Art Nouveau lived mostly in architecture, interiors, jewelry, glass, posters and illustration: the stuff of daily life. The American glassmaker Louis Comfort Tiffany worked in it, and so did the Czech designer Alphonse Mucha. The goal was deliberate: a brand-new style, instead of the copies of past styles that filled so much 19th-century art. Siegfried Bing's Paris gallery, called L'Art Nouveau ("new art"), helped give it its name.

cards.fact: Of Guimard's 141 Métro entrances, only 86 survive.
cards.context: At first, Parisians scorned them and called the lettering un-French. After 1910, Art Nouveau looked old-fashioned and was generally abandoned, and many entrances were demolished before anyone thought to save them. Being new, it turns out, is the fastest way to become old. Now the survivors are treasured.

cards.headline: What Munch felt at sunset
cards.body: Munch wrote that he was out walking as the sun set, when the sky suddenly turned blood red. He stood there trembling with anxiety, and sensed an infinite scream passing through nature. His 1893 painting shows a swirling blood-red sky over the Oslo fjord, and a figure with wide eyes, an oval mouth and hands clamped over its ears. On this reading, it's hearing the scream, not making it.

cards.headline: Paint the feeling, not the view

title: Picasso and Cubism
objective: After this level you can explain how Cubism showed objects from many angles at once.
summary: Picasso and Braque's Cubism, named from a critic's jibe about cubes, showed several views at once, built on Cézanne, and invented collage.

cards.headline: In 1908, a critic sneered that Braque's houses were just cubes.
cards.body: Louis Vauxcelles meant it as a put-down: Georges Braque had turned a cluster of houses into a pile of blocks. The jibe became the name. Cubism, created mainly by Braque and Pablo Picasso in Paris between 1907 and 1914, became one of the most influential styles of the 20th century.

mascot.line: Don't be fooled by the name. Cubism isn't about cubes; it's several views at once.

cards.headline: Every side at once
cards.body: Hold a mug. From the front you see its side and handle; from above, a circle. A normal painting picks one view. The Cubists refused to choose: they showed several views of an object at once, broken into overlapping planes, like a mug reassembled from shards. Out went the old tricks for faking depth, perspective and shading. The picture admits it's flat, and shows you more than one eye could.

cards.headline: Cézanne's cones, taken further
cards.body: Remember Cézanne's cylinder, sphere and cone from Level 61? His landscapes deeply inspired the Cubists in their first stage. In Analytic Cubism (about 1910 to 1912) they took things apart into facets and kept the colors quiet: tan, brown, gray and cream. Their favorite subjects sat close at hand, like musical instruments, bottles, glasses and faces.

cards.fact: Then the Cubists started gluing real things into their pictures.
cards.context: After 1912, in Synthetic Cubism, they pasted materials like newspaper and tobacco wrappers onto the canvas beside painted areas. That's collage. A painting had always been a picture of the world. Now little pieces of the actual world were part of the painting.

title: Abstract Art
objective: After this level you can explain how Kandinsky and Mondrian left recognizable subjects behind.
summary: Kandinsky decided objects harmed his paintings; Mondrian reduced art to straight lines and primary colors; Hilma af Klint painted abstractly by 1906.

cards.headline: At dusk, Kandinsky saw a glowing painting he didn't recognize. It was his.
cards.body: In his memoir Reminiscences (1913), Wassily Kandinsky wrote that he came home at dusk and saw a beautiful picture of pure forms and colors, glowing. Then it clicked: it was one of his own paintings, standing on its side. With nothing recognizable in it, it glowed. From then on, he wrote, he knew for certain that "the object harmed my paintings".

cards.headline: Painting like music
cards.body: A tune can move you without showing you anything. Kandinsky wanted painting to do the same: colors, lines and shapes, freed from depicting objects, working as a visual language that could stir deep emotions. His claim to be first rests mainly on a watercolor dated 1910, a tangle of color patches and black lines. Experts now think it was actually made in 1913.

cards.headline: Mondrian strips it to the bones
cards.body: Piet Mondrian took abstraction toward strict order. His mature paintings use only straight horizontal and vertical lines, the primary colors (Level 4's red, yellow and blue), and black, white and gray. Picture a white canvas crossed by black bars, with a few rectangles filled in red, yellow or blue. In 1917 he cofounded De Stijl, a movement built on the most basic elements.

cards.fact: A Swedish painter was making abstract works by 1906, years before Kandinsky.
cards.context: Textbooks long dated the birth of abstraction to about 1910 to 1913 and credited Kandinsky. But Hilma af Klint was painting abstract works in her Stockholm studio as early as 1906. She asked that at least 20 years pass after her death before her work was shown, and she died in 1944. The story of who came first is still being rewritten.

title: Dada
objective: After this level you can explain Dada's protest against art and Duchamp's ready-mades.
summary: Dada began in wartime Zurich in 1916. Duchamp's Fountain, a urinal refused in 1917, made choosing an object into an artistic act: the readymade.

cards.headline: In 1917, an art show open to anyone who paid turned down a urinal.
cards.body: The Society of Independent Artists in New York took entries for a fee. Then a white porcelain urinal arrived, signed "R. Mutt". The artist was Marcel Duchamp, using a false name, and he was one of the society's founding members. It was refused anyway.

cards.headline: Dada: a nonsense name for a senseless time
cards.body: Duchamp's stunt belonged to Dada, which began in 1916 at Hugo Ball's Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich, in the middle of World War I. Its artists felt disgust for comfortable bourgeois values and despair over the war, and they distrusted the rational thinking they believed had led to it. The name, in the widely told account, came from a paper knife stuck at random into a dictionary: dada, French for "hobby-horse".

mascot.line: The word to keep is "chose". For a readymade, the choosing is the art.

cards.headline: The readymade: art by choosing
cards.body: Duchamp coined the word readymade for artworks made from manufactured objects he chose. His first, Bicycle Wheel (1913), is a bicycle wheel mounted on a stool. The key act was the choice. A 1917 defense of Fountain put it in capitals: "He CHOSE it." He took an ordinary object and placed it so its useful meaning disappeared under a new title.

cards.fact: In 2004, 500 art experts voted Fountain the most influential modern artwork.
cards.context: The original is lost. We know it from a 1917 photograph by Alfred Stieglitz, and museums show later replicas. Yet artists, curators, critics and dealers ranked it above Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. A urinal that was refused in 1917 ended up winning the argument.

title: Surrealism
objective: After this level you can explain how the Surrealists painted dreams, from Dalí to Magritte.
summary: Breton's 1924 manifesto sent Surrealists into dreams and the unconscious: Dalí's melting watches and Magritte's pipe that is not a pipe.

cards.headline: Salvador Dalí said his famous melting watches began with a soft Camembert.
cards.body: Take that with a pinch of salt, but take the idea seriously. The Surrealists went looking for art in dreams and the hidden parts of the mind, where watches can melt like cheese.

cards.headline: A manifesto for dreams
cards.body: In 1924 the poet André Breton published the Manifesto of Surrealism. Drawing on Sigmund Freud, he saw the unconscious mind as the wellspring of imagination, and he wanted dream and fantasy joined to everyday reality. Surrealism grew mainly out of Dada (Level 68), but where Dada said no, Surrealism tried to build something. Some Surrealists drew automatically, letting images spill out without censoring them.

cards.headline: Dalí: The Persistence of Memory
cards.body: It's small: 24 by 33 cm, not much bigger than a sheet of printer paper. Painted in 1931, it shows the coast of Catalonia, Dalí's home. Pocket watches have gone soft, one sagging over a ledge, and a strange, distorted face lies in the middle. Everything is painted realistically, which makes the impossible look real. Dalí even declared that he didn't know what it meant.

mascot.line: This is Level 3's painted porcupine again: a picture of a thing isn't the thing.

cards.fact: Magritte painted a pipe and wrote under it: "This is not a pipe."
cards.context: The Treachery of Images (1929), by René Magritte, shows a plain pipe above the French words Ceci n'est pas une pipe. It sounds like a riddle, but he explained it simply: nobody could fill or smoke the pipe in his picture. It's a picture of a pipe. That's Surrealism's quieter trick: making you doubt the ordinary.

title: Japanese Woodblock Prints
objective: After this level you can explain how ukiyo-e prints were made, including Hokusai's Great Wave.
summary: Ukiyo-e, 'pictures of the floating world', were cheap Edo-period prints made by a team, one block per color. Hokusai's Great Wave (about 1830-32) hides Mount Fuji in its hollow.

cards.headline: The most famous wave in art was made by a team of four.
cards.body: Katsushika Hokusai designed it, but a publisher, a carver and a printer turned his drawing into a print. It's a Japanese woodblock print, and prints like it were made cheaply and in large numbers.

cards.headline: Pictures of the floating world
cards.body: Ukiyo-e means "pictures of the floating world". The floating world was the theater and pleasure districts of Japanese cities in the Edo period (1615–1868). The prints showed its celebrities: kabuki actors and courtesans, the style icons of their day. Later came landscapes, sold as travel souvenirs. Woodblocks made them cheap and plentiful, more like posters than treasures. (Today they're treasures.)

cards.headline: A print takes a team
cards.body: A publisher organized each print and sold it. An artist drew the design in ink. A carver pasted that drawing face down on a block of cherry wood and cut straight through it, usually destroying it. So the first thing the carver did to the design was cut it up. Every color then got its own carved block. Marks called kento kept the colors lined up, and a printer inked each block and rubbed the paper onto it with a flat pad called a baren.

cards.fact: In the Great Wave, the famous mountain is one of the smallest things in the picture.
cards.context: Hokusai was about 70 when he made Under the Wave off Kanagawa, about 1830–32, for his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. A huge wave rears up, its foam breaking into claw-like fingers, over three boats of rowers. Far behind them, Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, sits small in the hollow under the wave. The series is named for Fuji, and Hokusai makes you hunt for it.

title: Chinese Calligraphy
objective: After this level you can explain why calligraphy is a major art form in China.
summary: Calligraphy (shufa) has been China's supreme visual art since the 3rd century CE: no touching up, thought to reveal character. Wang Xizhi's Orchid Pavilion Preface survives only in copies.

cards.headline: In China, the greatest visual art was handwriting.
cards.body: For centuries, calligraphy has ranked above painting. To see why, you need a brush, some ink and no second chances.

cards.headline: Four treasures, one take
cards.body: Calligraphy, shufa in Chinese, has been considered supreme among China's visual arts since the 3rd century CE. It needs four tools, honored as the Four Treasures of the Study: brush, ink, paper and inkstone. And it has one hard rule: no touching up. Go back over a weak stroke and, once the ink dries, the correction shows darker than the rest. Every stroke is a live performance with no retakes.

cards.headline: Writing that shows who you are
cards.body: Calligraphy is also regarded as uniquely revealing: it's thought to show the character and cultivation of the writer. Painters used the same brush and ink, and both arts were judged by similar standards, above all the life in the brushstroke itself. Your handwriting was, in a sense, your portrait.

cards.fact: China's most famous calligraphy may be in an emperor's tomb.
cards.context: In 353, Wang Xizhi, traditionally called the Sage of Calligraphy, wrote the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion. The story goes that he wrote it tipsy, then tried a thousand times to rewrite it and never matched the original. Legend says the Tang emperor Taizong loved it so much that it was buried with him. Today it's known only through copies.

title: Art of Africa
objective: After this level you can describe the Benin Bronzes and masks and the roles they played.
summary: The Benin Bronzes were court art for the oba's palace and altars, looted in 1897; some have been returned. A mask is one part of a masquerade, like the Yoruba Egungun.

cards.headline: A mask on a museum wall is like one frame cut from a film.
cards.body: In many African traditions, a mask is only one part of a masquerade: a performance with a full costume, music and dance. This level looks at two traditions from Nigeria on their own terms: the brass art of the Kingdom of Benin, and the masquerade.

cards.headline: Brass for a king
cards.body: The Kingdom of Benin, in today's Edo State, Nigeria (not the modern country called Benin), flourished from the 13th to the 19th century under its oba, or king. His brass casters formed a royal guild, Igun Eronmwon, the highest-ranking in the palace. They cast by lost wax: shape the piece in wax over a clay core, coat it in clay, heat it so the wax runs out, then pour molten metal into the gap. The guild still works on Igun Street in Benin City.

cards.headline: Made for a palace, not a gallery
cards.body: These works are called the Benin Bronzes, though most are brass, and the name also covers ivory, wood and more. Brass relief plaques, arranged to tell the court's story, were nailed onto the pillars of the oba's palace. Brass heads stood on royal ancestral altars, holding up carved ivory tusks. They had jobs: recording a court and honoring its ancestors.

cards.fact: In 1897, British forces took thousands of these works from Benin City.
cards.context: A British force invaded the city, burned it and looted the royal palace. The objects scattered to museums and collections abroad. In 2022 Germany transferred ownership of more than 1,100 Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, and the Smithsonian transferred 29. Many other museums, including the British Museum, still hold large collections, and calls for their return continue.

cards.headline: When the mask moves
cards.body: Masqueraders may embody spirits or ancestors. The audience knows a person is inside, yet accepts that the spirit is present. In Yoruba Egungun masquerades, the performer vanishes under layers of fine cloth and becomes a returned ancestor. When he spins, the cloth panels flare open. On a museum stand, nothing flares.

summary: Matisse, Derain and Vlaminck collected African sculpture; in 1907 Picasso studied masks at the Trocadero. But the works' makers, like Olowe of Ise, were rarely named.

cards.headline: In 1906, Matisse walked into a Paris shop and bought a small African figure.
cards.body: He showed it to Picasso. Within a year, Picasso was studying African masks in a Paris museum. But the famous story usually skips a question: who made these works?

cards.headline: Paris looks at Africa
cards.body: The figure Matisse bought was a small Vili carving from Central Africa. He, Derain and Vlaminck were early collectors of African sculpture. In 1907 Picasso spent time among the African masks and figures at the Trocadéro ethnographic museum in Paris. Afterwards he repainted faces in the big canvas he was working on, Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, so they looked like masks. The masks were in the painting now.

cards.headline: What Paris didn't ask
cards.body: Many of the Trocadéro's African objects had flowed in from France's colonies, piling up like a giant curiosity cabinet. Remember Level 74: in 1897, British forces carried thousands of works out of Benin City. Collectors usually labeled African works by people or "tribe", not by artist, and the modernists responded mainly to their forms, not their meanings. Admiring a shape isn't the same as knowing a work.

title: Aboriginal Art
objective: After this level you can describe Aboriginal rock art and dot painting and the stories they carry.
summary: A Kimberley kangaroo about 17,300 years old was dated by wasp nests. Western Desert dot painting began at Papunya in 1971; dots can veil sacred designs.

cards.headline: Australia's oldest known painting was dated with help from wasps.
cards.body: Well, from their nests. It's a kangaroo painted on a rock-shelter ceiling about 17,300 years ago, and it opens a story that runs right up to paintings made today.

mascot.line: This is Level 10's minimum age again, now with a maximum from the nests below.

cards.fact: The kangaroo is about 17,300 years old, Australia's oldest known intact rock painting.
cards.context: About 2 meters long, it stretches across the ceiling of a rock shelter in the Kimberley, on Balanggarra Country. Remember Level 10's minimum ages? Here, mud wasps built nests both under and over the paint. Radiocarbon from nests beneath gives a maximum age; nests on top give a minimum. The painting is squeezed in between. The dating was done with the permission and involvement of Traditional Owners.

cards.headline: Painting the Jukurrpa
cards.body: Many desert paintings depict ancestral stories. In Warlpiri the word is Jukurrpa, often translated as the Dreaming: the creation era when ancestral beings shaped the land and laid down the law. In 1971 at Papunya, in the Northern Territory, men led by Kaapa Tjampitjinpa painted a Honey Ant Dreaming mural on the school wall, encouraged by teacher Geoffrey Bardon. Soon they were painting their stories on boards. In 1972 they formed their own company, Papunya Tula Artists.

cards.headline: Dots that veil
cards.body: As the paintings reached wider audiences, artists increasingly used dots to cover secret and sacred designs, so a story could be shared without showing what outsiders shouldn't see. The dots are a veil, not just decoration. And they belong to the Western Desert around Papunya. Many other Aboriginal nations have their own, different visual languages, and some artists object when dots stand in for everyone.

objective: After this level you can describe Maya, Aztec and Inca art and building.
summary: Maya stelae carved rulers and dates in stone. The Mexica (Aztec) Sun Stone shows the current world era but can't tell the date. Inca walls fit without mortar; fine cloth beat gold.

cards.headline: The most famous "calendar" in the Americas can't tell you the date.
cards.body: It's a giant carved stone disc made by the Mexica, the people often called the Aztecs. Before we decode it, meet the Maya, who carved their kings in stone. Afterwards, meet the Inca, who built walls without mortar.

cards.headline: Maya: rulers in stone
cards.body: In Maya cities, rulers had themselves carved into history. Classic Maya stelae are free-standing stone slabs carved in relief, usually with a ruler's portrait beside hieroglyphic texts that name the ruler and record dates and deeds. Copán, in today's Honduras, is famous for massive, highly detailed ones. A stela was a monument and a press release in one.

cards.headline: The Sun Stone
cards.body: The Mexica Sun Stone is a basalt disc about 3.6 meters across, probably carved between 1502 and 1521. In December 1790 it was found buried face down in Mexico City's main plaza, built over the heart of the Mexica capital, Tenochtitlan. The face at its center is traditionally read as the sun god Tonatiuh; some scholars see the earth deity Tlaltecuhtli, or a blend of both. The design shows the current world era, 4 Movement, which the Mexica believed would end in earthquakes.

mascot.line: Its nickname says calendar, but it can't count days. Don't let a nickname do your thinking.

cards.fact: Nicknamed the Calendar Stone, it cannot tell you the date.
cards.context: Soon after it was found, the scholar Antonio de León y Gama read it as a timekeeping device, and that view held for about a century. But its twenty day signs have no numbers attached, so it can't count days. Many scholars now think it served as an altar.

cards.headline: Inca: walls and cloth
cards.body: Inca builders fitted stones without mortar, so precisely that even a thin knife blade can't slip between them. When an earthquake struck Cusco in 1650, most Spanish colonial buildings crumbled, while Inca walls and foundations survived nearly intact. Yet the most prized Inca art wasn't stone. It was cloth: the finest, called qompi, was more precious to the Inca than gold or silver.

title: Mexican Muralism
objective: After this level you can explain how Diego Rivera and others painted history on public walls.
summary: From 1921 Mexico commissioned murals on public buildings to teach history to all. Rivera's fresco History of Mexico climbs the National Palace; his Rockefeller mural was destroyed.

cards.headline: In 1921, Mexico's government started handing its painters the walls.
cards.body: After the Mexican Revolution, the country wanted to teach its own history to everyone, including people who couldn't read. So it gave artists the walls of public buildings.

cards.headline: History for everyone
cards.body: The education minister, José Vasconcelos, commissioned murals on public buildings to teach Mexico's history to a largely illiterate population. Three painters led the movement, known as los tres grandes, the Three Great Ones: Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros. Rivera had painted in a Cubist style in Europe beside friends like Picasso and Braque, then studied frescoes in Italy. Wall paintings won him over: anyone could see them, gallery or no gallery.

cards.headline: A staircase through history
cards.body: In true fresco, pigment goes onto wet lime plaster and becomes part of the wall as it dries. Between 1929 and 1935 Rivera painted The History of Mexico across three walls of the National Palace stairwell in Mexico City. It opens in the ancient Valley of Mexico, with a pyramid and people grinding maize and making art, then runs through the Spanish conquest to an imagined future. As you climb the stairs, you climb through history.

cards.fact: Rivera's New York mural was destroyed over one face: Lenin's.
cards.context: In 1933 Rivera painted a mural at Rockefeller Center in New York and included a portrait of Lenin. Nelson Rockefeller objected; Rivera refused to remove it. The unfinished mural was covered, then destroyed in 1934. Rivera painted the design again in Mexico City, at the Palace of Fine Arts. Public walls carry powerful messages, and start public fights.

title: Frida Kahlo
objective: After this level you can describe Kahlo's self-portraits and the symbols in them.
summary: Hurt in a 1925 bus accident, Kahlo learned to paint from a mirror over her bed and made 55 self-portraits. The Two Fridas and her thorn necklace self-portrait are built from symbols.

cards.headline: Frida Kahlo's favorite subject was the one in the mirror.
cards.body: She painted 55 self-portraits. To see why, start with a bus ride in 1925.

cards.headline: A mirror over the bed
cards.body: In 1925, at 18, Kahlo was badly injured in a bus accident: her spine and other bones were broken, and she spent months in plaster casts. Stuck in bed, she taught herself to paint, working from a mirror fixed to the canopy above her. She said she painted herself because she was so often alone and was the subject she knew best. Her brilliantly colored self-portraits deal with identity, the body and death.

cards.headline: Two Fridas, one artery
cards.body: In 1939, after separating from Diego Rivera, whom she had married in 1929, Kahlo painted The Two Fridas. Two Kahlos sit side by side. One wears a white European-style dress; the other wears traditional Tehuana dress, which Kahlo often wore. Their exposed hearts are joined by an artery. The European Frida has cut it with scissors, and blood stains her skirt. The Tehuana Frida holds a tiny portrait of Rivera.
cards.callout: The two dresses are often read as her European and Mexican heritage.

cards.fact: Every object in her 1940 self-portrait is a clue, and scholars read the clues differently.
cards.context: In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a necklace of thorns digs into her neck, a dead hummingbird hanging from it. A black cat and a monkey appear behind her shoulders. The thorns can recall Christ's crown of thorns; dead hummingbirds were Mexican folk charms for luck in love. Often called a Surrealist, Kahlo distanced herself from the label: she said she painted her own reality, not dreams.

cards.fact: The "Japanese" blue that dazzled Europe was European.

By the early 1800s it was made more cheaply in China and reached Japan, where it was called bero, from the Dutch for "Berlin blue". Hokusai used it all through Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, including the Great Wave. Europeans who admired the prints often took that blue for a traditional Japanese color.

title: Abstract Expressionism
objective: After this level you can explain how Pollock and Rothko made the act of painting the subject.
summary: Pollock poured paint on canvas laid on the floor, so the canvas became an arena to act in. Rothko painted glowing fields of color about basic human emotions.

cards.headline: In 1950, Jackson Pollock painted a picture 17 feet wide without an easel.
cards.body: He spread the canvas flat across his studio floor, then walked around it, pouring and flicking paint. The result, Autumn Rhythm, is a dense web of tangled lines with no top, no middle and nothing you could name. So what is it a picture of?

cards.headline: Painting from inside the picture
cards.body: Pollock worked on unstretched canvas laid on the floor, about 17 feet by 8. He poured, dripped and flicked thinned paint, moving around it from all sides, using sticks, trowels and knives more than brushes. Layer by layer, the lines built up into a dense web. Forget a painter dabbing at an easel; picture someone circling a table, very carefully, for weeks.

mascot.line: Keep this answer for any Pollock: the picture is a record of the act that made it.

cards.fact: A critic said the canvas had become an arena to act in.
cards.context: Harold Rosenberg called Pollock's circle "action painters": the canvas was an arena in which to act. So the subject of the picture is the act that made it. You're looking at a record of movement. The movement, Abstract Expressionism, began in New York in the late 1940s and shifted the center of modern painting from Paris to New York.

cards.headline: Rothko: the quiet side
cards.body: Not every Abstract Expressionist flung paint. Mark Rothko painted two or three soft-edged rectangles of color that nearly fill a wall-sized canvas, in thin paint, for quiet, almost meditative effects. He said his subject was basic human emotions: tragedy, ecstasy, doom. His last big project was a set of dark paintings, browns, maroons and blacks, for a chapel in Houston open to all faiths. It opened in 1971; Rothko had died in 1970.

title: Pop Art
objective: After this level you can explain how Pop Art borrowed from ads, comics and celebrity.
summary: Pop Art took its images from ads, packaging, films and comics, and dropped Abstract Expressionism's personal feelings. Lichtenstein painted comic panels, dots and all.

cards.headline: In 1956, a collage showed a bodybuilder holding a giant lollipop labeled POP.
cards.body: Richard Hamilton made it in London, for an exhibition called This Is Tomorrow, from pictures cut out of American magazines. Around the bodybuilder, a crowded living room is stuffed with modern stuff. Tomorrow, it turned out, looked a lot like a magazine ad.

cards.headline: Art from the supermarket
cards.body: Pop Art emerged in Britain and America in the 1950s and flourished in the 1960s. Its images came from places you didn't expect in a museum: advertising, product packaging, Hollywood movies, pop music and comic books. In 1957 Hamilton even wrote a list of what Pop should be, including popular, expendable, low cost, mass produced, witty and big business. That's a strange wish list for a work of art. It's a perfect one for a soda.

cards.headline: Why so impersonal?
cards.body: Remember Rothko from Level 81, painting tragedy and ecstasy? Pop turned the volume down. By choosing impersonal, everyday images, Pop artists moved away from the personal feelings that Abstract Expressionism was built on. A soup can has no inner torment. That was the point.

cards.fact: Roy Lichtenstein turned one comic panel into a painting.
cards.context: His Whaam! (1963) comes from a panel in a 1962 war comic, All-American Men of War. On the left panel, a fighter jet fires; on the right, the enemy plane explodes under the word WHAAM!. He copied the look of cheap printing: thick black outlines around areas of primary color, and Benday dots, the dot patterns printers used. The twist: he made those dots by hand, with a scrub brush and a homemade metal screen.

title: Warhol
objective: After this level you can describe Warhol's repeated images and his studio, the Factory.
summary: Warhol repeated soup cans and celebrities, printing photos with silkscreen. His silver studio was called the Factory, and he said he wanted to be a machine.

cards.headline: In 1962, a Los Angeles gallery lined up 32 soup cans. Painted ones.
cards.body: Andy Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans: 32 canvases, one for each flavor Campbell's sold, set on narrow ledges along the wall like groceries on a shelf. You could walk the aisle. Warhol was just getting started on repeating himself.

mascot.line: This is Level 39's print idea again: one design, printed over and over.

cards.headline: The art of the copy
cards.body: Warhol had spent about a decade as a commercial illustrator in New York, so he knew how ads work: show it again, and again. Soon he was using photographic silkscreen, a stencil printing process that can print the same image over and over. Instead of painting a face, he could print a photograph of it, as many times as he liked. The picture was the same every time. The point was that it was the same every time.

cards.fact: Marilyn Diptych repeats one face 50 times.
cards.context: Warhol made it in the weeks after Marilyn Monroe died in August 1962, from a single publicity photo. On the left, 25 bright Marilyns in color. On the right, 25 in black and white, some smeared, some fading almost to nothing. Nobody has to tell you it's about more than a movie star.

cards.headline: The Factory
cards.body: Warhol's New York studio had a fitting name: the Factory. From 1964 it was covered in silver foil and silver paint by his collaborator Billy Name, and it filled with underground film stars, rock musicians and hangers-on. In a 1963 interview Warhol said he wanted to be a machine, and that somebody else should be able to do all his paintings for him. For an artist, a strange ambition. For a factory, the job description.

title: Minimalism
objective: After this level you can explain Minimalism's plain shapes and industrial materials.
summary: Minimalism made simple geometric shapes that refer to nothing but themselves, often built by fabricators from industrial materials. Andre's bricks caused a 1976 uproar.

cards.headline: In 1976, British newspapers erupted over a museum's pile of bricks.
cards.body: The Tate had bought it in 1972: 120 firebricks, laid in two neat layers in a rectangle. When the papers found out, a public furor followed. To see why a museum wanted bricks at all, you need Minimalism.

cards.headline: Nothing but the thing
cards.body: Minimalism was an extreme form of abstract art that grew up in the USA in the 1960s: simple geometric shapes, often squares and rectangles. Its artists found Action painting too personal. A work of art, they said, shouldn't refer to anything but itself. The painter Frank Stella put it plainly in 1964: "What you see is what you see." No story, no hidden feeling, no symbol.
cards.callout: Pollock: the canvas records a gesture. Minimalism: the object is just the object.

cards.headline: Made by someone else, on purpose
cards.body: Donald Judd took the artist's hand out too. Professional fabricators built his works in industrial materials like galvanized iron and Plexiglas. His stacks, begun in 1965, are identical boxes hung one above another up a wall, at equal gaps. Picture a set of drawers floating up the wall with the cabinet taken away.

cards.fact: The bricks are just bricks. That's the art.
cards.context: Carl Andre's Equivalent VIII (1966) doesn't stand for a wall or a tomb or anything else: 120 firebricks, two layers, one rectangle, sitting on the floor. That's exactly what Minimalism asked for, and exactly what made the 1976 row so loud. The argument was the one from Level 2 all over again: is it art if it doesn't look like anything?

title: Conceptual Art
objective: After this level you can explain art where the idea matters more than the object.
summary: In conceptual art the idea matters most. LeWitt's wall drawings are instructions others carry out; Kosuth shows one chair as an object, a photo and a definition.

cards.headline: In 2008, a museum filled its walls with new drawings by the late Sol LeWitt.
cards.body: He had died the year before. A team of assistants, students and local artists drew them over nearly six months. Nobody was faking anything. For LeWitt, the drawing on the wall was never the real artwork.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: here, the idea outranks the object.

cards.headline: The idea is the machine
cards.body: Conceptual art is art in which the idea matters more than the finished object; it took off in the 1960s. In 1967 LeWitt wrote that the idea is the most important part of the work: "the idea becomes a machine that makes the art." His wall drawings are instructions, often with a diagram. Assistants carry them out on the wall, so each version comes out slightly different, like two cooks following the same recipe.

cards.fact: One chair, shown three ways.
cards.context: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs (1965) puts a real wooden folding chair next to a photograph of a chair and an enlarged dictionary definition of the word chair. Kosuth didn't make the chair, take the photo or write the definition; he chose and arranged them. Each is a different kind of chair: a thing you can sit on, a picture of one, and a set of words. So which one is the chair? The object, the picture or the idea? Where the art lives is the question.

title: Photography as Art
objective: After this level you can describe how photographers like Ansel Adams made photography a fine art.
summary: Early art photographers made photos look like paintings. Group f/64, with Ansel Adams, made sharpness the point instead, and in 1940 MoMA opened a photography department.

cards.headline: In 1941, Ansel Adams got one chance at a moonrise over a New Mexico village.
cards.body: He couldn't find his light meter, so he worked out the exposure from the brightness of the moon. Before he could make a second negative, the light left the crosses in the village graveyard. That one negative became Moonrise, Hernandez: a white moon over a black sky. Yet for decades, people had argued whether a photo could be art at all.

cards.headline: First, look like a painting
cards.body: In the early 1900s, photographers who wanted respect imitated other arts. The Photo-Secession, founded in 1902 with Alfred Stieglitz, promoted Pictorialism: working on negatives and prints so they looked like drawings, etchings and oil paintings. Stieglitz argued that photography was a fine art, equal to painting. The catch: to count as art, a photo had to look like something else.

cards.headline: Then, look like a photograph
cards.body: In 1932 Adams, Edward Weston and others in San Francisco formed Group f/64. The name is a camera setting: a tiny lens opening that keeps everything sharp, with fine detail. They wanted "straight" photography, crisp and unashamed of being a photo. Where the Pictorialists borrowed painting's look, f/64 bet on what only a camera could do.

cards.fact: One negative, many different prints.
cards.context: Adams printed Moonrise many times over the years, and they weren't identical: he kept raising the contrast, making the moon whiter and the sky darker. The picture was made in the darkroom as much as in the field. Museums noticed. In 1940, working closely with Adams, Beaumont Newhall founded a department of photography at New York's Museum of Modern Art.

title: Land Art and Installations
objective: After this level you can describe art made from landscapes and from whole rooms.
summary: Land art is made in the landscape itself: Spiral Jetty is a rock coil that the Great Salt Lake hides and reveals. Installations fill rooms, like Kusama's mirror rooms.

cards.headline: You can't hang Spiral Jetty on a wall. For 30 years, you couldn't even see it.
cards.body: It's a coil of black rock 1,500 feet long, curling counterclockwise out from the shore of Utah's Great Salt Lake. Robert Smithson built it in 1970. In 1972 the lake rose over it, and it stayed under until 2002.

cards.headline: Art made of the land
cards.body: Land art is made directly in the landscape, from earth or natural materials like rocks. It was part of the wider conceptual art movement of the 1960s and 1970s; remember LeWitt in Level 85, where the idea outranked the saleable object? Spiral Jetty is about 6,000 tons of black basalt rock and earth from the site itself. No gallery could hold it, and no collector could carry it home.

cards.fact: The lake is part of the artwork.
cards.context: Smithson built the jetty while the water was low. In 1972 it disappeared beneath the lake. Droughts brought it back in 2002, and it has been visible since, made of mud, salt crystals, rocks and water. Its look depends on the weather and the water level. That's not a flaw in the work; it's the work being outdoors.

cards.headline: Installation: art you walk into
cards.body: Installation art often fills a whole room that you walk through, so you're inside the work, not in front of it. Yayoi Kusama's first mirror room, Infinity Mirror Room: Phalli's Field (1965), filled a closed room with soft stuffed forms covered in red polka dots. title: Street Art
objective: After this level you can explain how graffiti and street art moved from walls into galleries.
summary: Haring drew in chalk in the subway and Basquiat wrote SAMO on walls before both became gallery stars. Banksy works in stencils, and one of his canvases shredded itself at auction.

cards.headline: In 2018, a Banksy sold at auction, then shredded itself.
cards.body: Just after the sale, Girl with Balloon slid partway down through a shredder hidden in its own frame. Instead of a disaster, it became a new artwork, Love Is in the Bin. So how did art from the street end up in an auction room?

cards.headline: Chalk on the subway
cards.body: From 1980 to 1985, Keith Haring drew in New York's subway: white chalk on the black paper that covered unrented advertising panels. It was illegal, so he drew fast, and he was arrested many times. He made hundreds of these drawings, maybe thousands. Your commute, with an art show on the wall.

cards.headline: From SAMO to the gallery
cards.body: In the late 1970s, Jean-Michel Basquiat and his friend Al Diaz spray-painted cryptic sayings on walls in Lower Manhattan, signed SAMO. They were slogans and jokes, not just a name. Around 1980 Basquiat dropped SAMO to paint, and by the early 1980s his paintings were being shown around the world. The wall was his first gallery.

mascot.line: Same method as Level 5's hand stencils, just on a city wall and built for speed.

cards.fact: Banksy works in stencils, for speed.
cards.context: Banksy, an anonymous British artist, has used stencils since 2000 to work faster, building a cast of images like rats and policemen. Remember Level 5? Blow pigment over a hand and its outline stays on the rock. A street stencil works the same way: spray over a cut-out shape and it stays on the wall. The payoff came indoors: in 2018 Girl with Balloon sold at Sotheby's for $1.4 million, just before it shredded.

title: Art and Money
objective: After this level you can explain why a few artworks sell for hundreds of millions of dollars.
summary: The Salvator Mundi went from a damaged auction find to $450.3 million in 2017, thanks to a disputed attribution to Leonardo and two determined bidders.

cards.headline: In 2005, two dealers bought a battered painting of Christ at a small auction.
cards.body: It came from New Orleans, in bad shape and heavily overpainted. In 2017 the same painting, the Salvator Mundi, sold at Christie's in New York for $450.3 million, a record for any painting at auction. What changed?

cards.headline: The name on the label
cards.body: After cleaning and study, the painting was authenticated as a work by Leonardo da Vinci by 2011. Christie's called it one of fewer than 20 known paintings by him. Nobody can make more Leonardos, so each one is extraordinarily scarce. But not everyone agrees it is one: some specialists think Leonardo painted only parts of it, and others say the heavy restoration makes a firm verdict impossible.

cards.headline: Two bidders are enough
cards.body: An auction price isn't a label on a shelf; it's a contest. The Salvator Mundi bidding lasted about 19 minutes and came down to two bidders on the phone. The winning bid was $400 million, and fees brought the price to $450.3 million. At auction, a price keeps climbing only while someone else keeps bidding. It takes two to set a record.

cards.fact: Fame sells too.
cards.context: Remember Warhol's repeated Marilyns from Level 83? Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, a 1964 silkscreen of her face, sold at Christie's New York in May 2022 for $195 million, at the time the highest auction price for any 20th-century artwork. A rare name, a famous image and two determined bidders: that's the recipe for a record.

cards.headline: Each move answered the last
cards.body: Pop swapped Abstract Expressionism's personal feelings for impersonal, everyday images. Minimalism found Action painting too personal and cut art down to simple geometric shapes that refer to nothing but themselves. Conceptual art made the idea more important than the object, and land art, part of that wider movement, walked out of the gallery into the landscape.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this chapter: the object got lighter, the idea got heavier.

cards.fact: In 1968, two critics named the trend: the dematerialization of art.
cards.context: Lucy Lippard and John Chandler described "ultra-conceptual" art, where the idea matters more than the object. Look back along the timeline: paint on canvas, printed images, factory bricks, written instructions, a rock spiral in a lake. At almost every step, the object got lighter and the idea got heavier.

title: How to Read a Painting
objective: After this level you can use a simple method to look closely at any painting.
summary: Museum visitors average about 27 seconds per artwork. Feldman's four steps (describe, analyze, interpret, judge) slow you down; the Icarus painting shows why.

cards.headline: In 2001, visitors at the Met looked at each artwork for about 27 seconds.
cards.body: Researchers quietly timed people in front of the art at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. The average glance lasted about 27 seconds. Plenty of time for a quick verdict, not much for noticing things. Here's a painting that punishes a quick look, and a method for a slow one.

cards.headline: Find the boy who fell from the sky
cards.body: In Greek myth, Icarus flew on wings of feathers and wax, went too near the Sun, and fell into the sea. So Landscape with the Fall of Icarus, from about 1560, should be all about him. Instead you see a farmer ploughing a hillside, a daydreaming shepherd, a passing ship. Icarus? Just a pair of legs in the water near the ship, lower right. A casual glance misses him completely. (Many scholars think this Brussels canvas is an early copy of a lost Bruegel original.)

mascot.line: The rule to keep: describe first, judge last.

cards.headline: Four steps, in order
cards.body: Art educator Edmund Burke Feldman gave teachers a four-step method. Describe: say only what you see, down to line, shape, color and texture. Analyze: how do those parts work together, and where does your eye go? Interpret: what might it mean? Judge: does it succeed, and why? Keep your opinion for the end. Careful description comes first because every other step is built on it.

cards.fact: One painting, more than one reading.
cards.context: Interpret the Icarus painting and you have choices. One common reading: ordinary life carries on, unmoved, while someone drowns, and the ploughman, shepherd and ship never notice. Britannica sees a moral too: pride and ambition come before a fall. Neither is written on the canvas. Both come from looking long enough to find those legs.

title: Composition
objective: After this level you can explain how artists guide your eye with balance, lines and a focal point.
summary: Composition steers your eye. Balance spreads visual weight, emphasis makes a focal point, movement leads you along lines, and the rule of thirds dates from 1797.

cards.headline: Bruegel painted a winter walk that your eyes take without asking.
cards.body: In Hunters in the Snow, from 1565, hunters trudge home through the snow with tired dogs and a single fox to show for it. Below them, the land drops away to frozen ponds full of skaters. You don't decide where to look next. The painting decides for you. Remember Feldman's Analyze step? This is what it's looking for.

cards.headline: Balance: a see-saw you can't see
cards.body: Getty's art educators call balance the spread of visual weight: objects, colors, textures and space. Picture a see-saw: when the weights balance, the design feels stable. In symmetrical balance, the two sides are alike, like a face. In asymmetrical balance, the sides are different but still look balanced. In radial balance, things are arranged around a central point, like spokes on a bike wheel.

cards.headline: Emphasis, then movement
cards.body: Emphasis is the part that catches your attention first, the focal point. Artists usually make it stand out by contrast: a different size, color, texture or shape. Movement is the path your eye takes next, pulled along lines, edges and colors. In Hunters in the Snow, a diagonal line of bare trees carries your eye from the hunters down the hill and into the distant landscape. Nobody told you to go there. You just went.

cards.fact: The "rule of thirds" was first written down in 1797.
cards.context: John Thomas Smith named it in a book for landscape painters, Remarks on Rural Scenery. Today it usually means: divide a picture into nine equal parts with two horizontal and two vertical lines, then put the important things along those lines or where they cross, rather than dead center. Even Smith offered it as a rule of thumb, not a law.

title: Symbols in Art
objective: After this level you can decode common symbols like skulls, lilies and dogs in older paintings.
summary: Old paintings speak in symbols: a skull says remember you must die, lilies mean purity, a dog may mean faithfulness. Symbols are clues to interpret, not a fixed code.

cards.headline: In 1533, Holbein hid a skull in plain sight.
cards.body: The Ambassadors shows two men posing side by side. Between their feet floats a long, smeared shape. From the front it's a puzzle. Look up at the painting from its bottom right corner, and the smear becomes a large skull. Holbein built the trick into the paint. Here's what the skull, and other symbols, were saying.

cards.headline: Skulls: remember you must die
cards.body: A skull is a memento mori, Latin for "remember you must die." Its partner is the vanitas still life: a table set with a skull, a snuffed-out candle, books, wine, a musical instrument. The message: life is short, and worldly pleasures are worthless in the end. These pictures became popular in the 1600s, in a religious age. So a still life with a skull isn't a menu. It's a warning.

cards.headline: Lilies and dogs
cards.body: White lilies generally stand for purity, which ties them to the Virgin Mary. In paintings of the Annunciation, the angel Gabriel often holds one, or it stands in a vase. Dogs can stand for faithfulness. In Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait of 1434, a small dog, every hair painted, stands at the couple's feet: likely a sign of faithfulness in marriage.

mascot.line: Don't hunt for a secret code. With symbols, "probably" is often the honest answer.

cards.fact: A symbol is a clue, not a code.
cards.context: Even London's National Gallery says the Arnolfini dog "may be intended" to stand for fidelity. Meanings also shift: lilies belong to saints such as Catherine of Siena too. So treat a symbol the way Level 91 taught: describe it first, then interpret it with evidence. Sometimes the best answer starts with "probably."

title: Museums
objective: After this level you can explain how museums began and what they do today.
summary: Public museums grew from private collections: the Ark (1634), the Ashmolean (1683), the British Museum (1753), the Louvre (1793). Today they research, collect, conserve and exhibit.

cards.headline: In 1793, revolutionaries opened a king's palace and let the public in.
cards.body: The Louvre in Paris began as a royal residence in 1546. In 1793, France's revolutionary government opened its Grande Galerie to the public as an art museum. Walking through a king's palace to look at his paintings: that was new. But the idea of a public museum was already more than a century old.

cards.headline: It started with a house full of wonders
cards.body: In 1634, two gardeners, John Tradescant and his son, also John, opened a museum in their home in Lambeth, south London. They called it the Ark. One visitor said you could see more curiosities there in a day than in a lifetime of travel. The collection even held a preserved dodo. Later the collection passed to Elias Ashmole, who gave it to Oxford University, where it became the heart of Britain's first public museum.
