title: Restoration
objective: After this level you can explain how conservators clean and repair old art.
summary: Conservators clean away discolored varnish and overpaint, and make every addition reversible. Borja's 2012 touch-up shows why; Ghent's Lamb shows what care can reveal.

cards.headline: In 2012, a well-meant touch-up turned a painting of Christ into a meme.
cards.body: In Borja, Spain, Cecilia Giménez, an amateur painter in her eighties, set out to restore Ecce Homo, a fresco of Christ in her local church. The result, whose head people said looked like a hairy monkey, was nicknamed "Monkey Christ" and went viral. The church foundation said she acted with the best intentions. Good intentions, it turns out, aren't a technique.

cards.headline: Step one: lift the fog
cards.body: Much of a conservator's work starts with cleaning off dirt and old varnish. Over time varnish discolors, laying a yellowish, foggy film over everything, so the colors you see aren't quite the ones the artist chose. Taking it off reveals the originals underneath. At London's National Gallery, one conservator removed 75 years' worth of discolored varnish from Rubens's landscape Het Steen. Same painting, suddenly different weather.

mascot.line: If you keep one rule from this level: whatever you add must be able to come off again.

cards.headline: The golden rule: it must come undone
cards.body: Today's conservators follow a rule the Borja touch-up ignored: anything they add must be reversible. Where paint is lost, London's National Gallery fills and retouches the gaps, and it makes sure all its work is reversible or removable, should future generations need to take it off. Past restorers didn't always think that way. If a future expert knows better, the original is still there.

cards.fact: Cleaning the Ghent Altarpiece gave a lamb a human face.
cards.context: Jan and Hubert van Eyck finished the altarpiece by 1432. Around 1550, other painters covered its Lamb of God with a calmer, more animal face. In 2019, conservators from Belgium's Royal Institute for Cultural Heritage removed that overpaint with solvents and scalpels. Out stared the original: forward-gazing eyes, a startlingly human look. The internet laughed. A 2020 study backed the conservators: that face is the van Eycks' own.

title: Forgery
objective: After this level you can explain how famous forgeries were made and caught.
summary: Forgers fake the look, but chemistry catches the materials: Bakelite and cobalt blue unmasked van Meegeren's Vermeers, and titanium white exposed Beltracchi.

cards.headline: In 1945, a Dutch painter's best defense was confessing to forgery.
cards.body: After the Second World War, a painting sold as a work by the 1600s Dutch master Johannes Vermeer turned up in the collection of Nazi leader Hermann Göring. Han van Meegeren, who had sold it, was arrested for collaborating with the Nazis, a serious charge. His defense: it wasn't a Vermeer. He had painted it himself.

cards.headline: A forger paints for the police
cards.body: Nobody believed him, so he proved it: watched by the authorities, he painted another "Vermeer" with the same materials and techniques. His tricks were clever. He took a real 1600s painting and scrubbed most of the picture off, careful to keep its old network of cracks. He mixed his paint with Bakelite, a synthetic resin, and baked the canvas so it set hard like old paint.

cards.headline: Caught by chemistry
cards.body: Tests by Paul Coremans, head of Belgium's central museum laboratory, found phenol-formaldehyde resin, Bakelite, in the paint. Bakelite was invented in 1907. Two paintings also held cobalt blue, a pigment not made until the 1800s. No painter of the 1600s could have used either. In 1947 van Meegeren was convicted of forgery and sentenced to one year in prison. He died of a heart attack before he served it.

mascot.line: Keep this: a forger can copy a style, but not a pigment from the future.

cards.fact: A forger's worst enemy is a paint that didn't exist yet.
cards.context: Wolfgang Beltracchi didn't copy famous pictures; he invented new ones "in the style of" artists such as Max Ernst and Heinrich Campendonk. Then a lab tested a "Campendonk" supposedly from 1914 and found titanium white, a pigment not yet in use in 1914. That one white unraveled the whole scheme. In 2011 he was sentenced to six years.

title: Stolen Art
objective: After this level you can describe famous art thefts, including the Mona Lisa in 1911.
summary: In 1911 a former Louvre worker stole the Mona Lisa; the theft made it world-famous. The 1990 Gardner Museum theft is still unsolved, and its empty frames still hang.

cards.headline: In August 1911, the Mona Lisa vanished from the Louvre.
cards.body: Leonardo da Vinci began her about 1503: a woman with a mysterious smile, set against a distant landscape. She hung in the Louvre in Paris. Then one morning she was gone. What happened next turned a respected painting into the most famous one on Earth.

cards.headline: An inside job
cards.body: The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian who had worked at the Louvre fitting glass over paintings. He hid in a closet overnight, took the portrait from the wall in the morning and walked off without suspicion. Paintings were often taken down for cleaning, so for over a day nobody noticed. Police went on to question suspects including Pablo Picasso, who was innocent.

cards.headline: The theft that made her famous
cards.body: Newspapers turned it into a sensation, and people flocked to the Louvre just to look at the empty space on the wall. In 1913 Peruggia tried to sell the painting to an art dealer in Florence, who alerted the police. It was found in the false bottom of his trunk. The Mona Lisa went back to Paris world-famous: the best publicity she ever got was being missing.

cards.fact: In Boston, empty frames have waited since 1990.
cards.context: In the early hours of March 18, 1990, two men dressed as police officers talked their way into the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, restrained the guards and took 13 works, including paintings by Rembrandt and Vermeer. The case is still unsolved, and the museum offers a $10 million reward. Empty frames still hang where the paintings were. Art this famous is nearly impossible to sell openly.

title: Digital Art
objective: After this level you can explain how computers and screens have changed the way art is made.
summary: Computer art began with plotter drawings in 1965. Nees's Schotter turned randomness into art, Cohen's AARON drew by itself, and in 2021 an NFT sold for $69.3 million.

cards.headline: In February 1965, a gallery in Stuttgart showed drawings made by a computer.
cards.body: Georg Nees, a mathematician working as a software engineer at Siemens, wrote programs, and a drawing machine turned them into ink on paper. It was one of the first shows of computer graphics anywhere. For the first time, an artist's main tool was a set of instructions.

cards.headline: Order, then chaos
cards.body: Picture Nees's Schotter ("gravel"), printed between 1968 and 1970. At the top, neat rows of squares sit perfectly straight. Row by row they tilt and slip a little more, until the bottom looks like a spilled box of tiles. Nees built random variables into his program, so the orderly squares descend into chaos. He was exploring order and disorder in a picture.

cards.headline: A program that draws by itself
cards.body: In 1973 the painter Harold Cohen started AARON, a program that made drawings on its own, following rules he wrote. Early on, a small robot "turtle" holding a marker crawled over the paper to draw them. For about 20 years Cohen colored the drawings by hand; AARON only learned to color them itself in 1995. So who's the artist: Cohen, AARON, or both?

cards.fact: In 2021, a digital file sold for $69.3 million.
cards.context: Mike Winkelmann, known as Beeple, made an image every day from 2007, then combined 5,000 of them into one collage. In March 2021 Christie's sold it as an NFT, a token on a blockchain that certifies ownership of a digital item, for $69.3 million: the first purely digital artwork sold that way by a major auction house. Remember Level 2's question: what counts as art? Screens reopened it.

title: Why Art Lasts
objective: After this level you can explain why some art stays meaningful for centuries.
summary: Art lasts when it survives, when people keep caring for and looking at it, and when new viewers find new meanings, as poets did with the Icarus painting.

cards.headline: Centuries after it was painted, the Icarus picture got a famous poem.
cards.body: In the winter of 1938, the poet W. H. Auden stood in the Brussels museum in front of Level 91's Landscape with the Fall of Icarus, and wrote a poem about it. Why do some paintings keep people talking for centuries while others vanish? Three reasons.

cards.headline: Reason 1: it survives
cards.body: First, the object has to make it. Lascaux's paintings lasted about 17,000 years in the dark, then about 15 years of visitors damaged them. Survival takes care, and careful care: that's why conservators now make every treatment reversible or removable, so no one's repair becomes the next generation's problem.

cards.headline: Reason 2: people keep looking
cards.body: Fame isn't fixed. Remember Level 97: the 1911 theft made the Mona Lisa world-famous, and people even flocked to the Louvre to see the empty wall where she had hung. One way to read that story: a work that is seen, talked about and argued over stays alive in a way a forgotten one doesn't.

cards.fact: Every new viewer can find a new painting.
cards.context: Auden read the Icarus picture as a scene of suffering happening while everyone else goes on with ordinary life. In the early 1960s, the American poet William Carlos Williams wrote his own poem on it, with its line "a splash quite unnoticed." Neither poet was wrong. Describe, analyze, interpret: every careful look adds a reading, and that's one way to see why art lasts.
